Superalgebra deformations of web categories: Affine and cyclotomic webs
Nicholas Davidson, Jonathan R. Kujawa, Robert Muth

Abstract
. Let 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} be a characteristic zero domain. We define and study a diagrammatic monoidal 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} -linear supercategory 𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝒜 aff \mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}} associated to any locally unital Frobenius 𝕜 \mathbbm{k} -superalgebra A A . This category can be viewed variously as an affinization of the finite web category 𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝒜 \mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}} previously defined by the authors and Zhu, as a thickening of the degenerate affine wreath product algebras defined by Savage, or as a Frobenius deformation of affine web categories defined by Song and Wang. We show that there is an asymptotically faithful family of functors from 𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝒜 aff \mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}} to the monoidal supercategory of endofunctors of 𝔤 ​ 𝔩 n ​ ( A ) \mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A) -modules for every n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 , and use this to establish a basis of ‘decorated double coset diagrams’ for morphism spaces in 𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝒜 aff \mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}} . We also define and establish basis results for the cyclotomic quotient category 𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝒜 Λ \mathbf{Web}^{\Lambda}_{\mathcal{A}} associated with a cyclotomic datum Λ \Lambda .



1.
Introduction

1.1.
Overview

The goal of the present paper is to pull together several strands of modern representation theory. Throughout, we work over an characteristic zero domain
\mathbbm{k}
.

The first strand is web categories. These are
\mathbbm{k}
-linear diagrammatic categories first introduced to describe certain categories of representations for Lie algebras
[
8
,
22
]
. They have since played a prominent role in Lie theory, algebraic combinatorics, combinatorial representation theory, low-dimensional topology, cluster algebras, and other areas, with the references too numerous to list.

The second strand is the degenerate affine wreath product algebra. Wreath product algebras naturally generalize the symmetric groups and share many of their nice representation theoretic features. In the past few decades it became clear the symmetric groups are part of a larger story that is revealed by viewing them as a cyclotomic quotient of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra. In particular, this point of view leads to categorical representation theory, categorification, and the algebras introduced by Khovanov–Lauda and Rouquier. These developments motivate recent work on degenerate affine wreath product algebras and related structures (e.g., see
[
7
,
15
,
23
,
24
,
26
,
27
,
33
]
and references therein).

The third strand is Schurification. Given an associative
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A=A_{\bar{0}}\oplus A_{\bar{1}}
and a subalgebra
\mathfrak{a}\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
, one can construct a
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
for any pair of natural numbers
n
and
d
. Let
V=A^{\oplus n}
. Then
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-form inside the algebra of endomorphisms of the wreath product
A\wr\mathfrak{S}_{d}
acting in the obvious way on
V^{\otimes d}
, where the choice of subalgebra
\mathfrak{a}
controls the
\mathbbm{k}
-form one obtains. Unlike the full endomorphism algebra, the
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
often has the well-behaved and interesting representation theory one expects from something which deserves to be called the Schur algebra associated to
A
(e.g., see
[
18
,
19
,
20
,
21
]
). The importance of this algebra is underscored by the fact that, as conjectured by Turner, the RoCK blocks of the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{d}
over a field
\mathbb{F}
of positive characteristic are Morita equivalent to
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)\otimes_{\mathbbm{Z}}\mathbb{F}

[
12
,
13
]
when
A
is the type
A
zigzag superalgebra defined over
\mathbbm{k}=\mathbbm{Z}
, see
Section

2.2.3
. Thus, these algebras control a significant portion of the modular representation theory of the symmetric groups. Similar statements are conjecturally true for the spin representations of the symmetric groups
[
16
, Conjecture 1]
and the classical Schur algebras
[
20
, Conjecture 7.58]
.

1.2.
Finite webs

Let
A=A_{\bar{0}}\oplus A_{\bar{1}}
be a locally unital superalgebra over
\mathbbm{k}
, with distinguished idempotents
I\subseteq A
.
Let
\mathfrak{a}\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
be locally unital even subalgebra, and assume there exists a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
\mathfrak{a}
that can be extended to a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis of
A
. This is, of course, automatic if
\mathbbm{k}
is a field and is a mild assumption in general. Write
\mathcal{A}
for the data
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
.

In
[
9
]
we introduced the web category
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
associated to this data. This is a diagrammatic
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal category defined via generators and relations. The objects are tuples of symbols of the form
i^{(x)}
, where
i\in I
and
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, with concatenation of words providing the monoidal product. The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given by the diagrams:

for
i,j\in I
,
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
, and
f\in jAi
if
z=1
and
f\in j\mathfrak{a}i
if
z\geq 2
. We call these the split, merge, crossing and coupon morphisms, respectively. Our convention is to read diagrams from bottom to top. Composition is given by vertical concatenation and the monoidal product is given by horizontal concatenation. Morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are then
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combinations of diagrams built by repeated concatenation of generating diagrams, subject to a fairly simple set of local relations.

To understand a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal category given by generators and relations, one would like an explicit
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for each morphism space. Doing so establishes that the morphism spaces have the expected size and that they do not contain torsion. Having an explicit basis also facilitates computations and proofs. A standard way of obtaining such bases in this setting is to define a representation of the category that is sufficiently faithful.

We did this for
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
in
[
9
]
. In that paper, we showed that for every
n\geq 1
, there exists a functor

G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A),

where
\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
is the category of right supermodules for the Lie superalgebra
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. On objects,
G_{n}(i^{(x)})=S^{x}({}_{i}V)
, where
{}_{i}V=(iA)^{\oplus n}
is the natural right (
i
-colored) supermodule for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
, and
S^{x}({}_{i}V)
is its
x
th symmetric power. On generating morphisms, the merge and split webs are sent to homomorphisms induced by the usual product and coproducts on the symmetric superalgebra of
{}_{i}V
, while the coupon labeled by
f\in jAi
is sent to the homomorphism given by left multiplication by
f
. In
Theorem

8.4.1
below we recall this functor more precisely.

We also showed that the family of functors
\{G_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}
is
asympotically faithful
in the sense that, for any nonzero morphism
\phi
in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
, there exists an
N
so that
G_{n}(\phi)\neq 0
for
n\geq N
. This allowed us to determine a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for the morphism spaces of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
. We also proved that
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
appears naturally in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
as an explicit sum of morphism spaces. In particular, this establishes a diagrammatic description for
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
. In addition, we obtained a Howe duality for the pair
\left(\mathfrak{gl}_{m}(A),\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)\right)
under the assumption that
\mathbbm{k}
is a field and
A
is semisimple, generalizing Howe dualities that appear in the literature.

1.3.
Affine webs

Assume that
\mathcal{A}=(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
is as above. In addition, assume that
A
is a Frobenius superalgebra (we in fact require the slightly more strict assumption that
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
constitutes a ‘great pair’; see
Section

2
for further details and examples).
In the present paper we introduce and study a (degenerate) affine web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
attached to the data
\mathcal{A}
, along with their cyclotomic quotients. This amounts to adding additional generators to
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
,

(1.3.1)

Definition

\mathbbm{k}

.

The squiggly green decoration is called a ‘teleporter’ and is shorthand for a certain collection of coupon morphisms (see
Section

4
). Here, nomen est omen: these teleporters satisfy remarkable properties (
Section

4.1
) inherited from the Frobenius structure of
A
. Our teleporters can be viewed as thickened analogues of those in
[
7
]
.

1.4.
Main results

Let
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
be the category of endofunctors of the category of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules. For
n\geq 1
, in
Theorem

9.5.1
we establish a monoidal functor,

H_{n}:\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)).

On generating objects,
H_{n}(x)=-\otimes S^{x}({}_{i}V)
. On generating morphisms the split, merge, crossing and coupon go to the obvious natural transformations that act on the symmetric powers, while the affine dots go to a map defined using a ‘thick’ Casimir tensor. We call this the
(symmetric) defining representation
of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. Moreover, we prove in Theorem
11.3.1
that this family of functors is asymptotically faithful, allowing us to determine a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis of ‘decorated double coset diagrams’ for the morphism spaces of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
in
Corollary

11.3.2
.

We also consider cyclotomic quotients of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. Given a
regular
cyclotomic datum
\Lambda
of level
\ell
, the cyclotomic quotient category
\mathbf{Web}^{\Lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}
is defined in
Section

12
, after which we establish that the morphism spaces are free
\mathbbm{k}
-modules with a basis consisting of those diagrams with fewer than
\ell
affine dots on a given strand. The regularity condition on our cyclotomic data is inconvenient to verify in specific examples, but it is required to establish our basis results when working integrally (over
\mathbbm{k}
). After proving our basis results, we finish
Section

12
by establishing the regularity condition holds in several important cases, including the case where
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero, or
\mathfrak{a}=A_{\bar{0}}
, or
A
is a zigzag algebra. Since these cover the examples of greatest interest to the authors, we leave the general case of when the regularity holds as an open question.

1.5.
Related works

As noted in this introduction,
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
can be be considered as an
affinization
of the finite web category
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
, and up to Morita equivalence,
affinization
of the Schurification
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
. In
[
27
]
, Savage constructed
(degenerate) affine wreath product algebras
associated to Frobenius algebras
A
, and their cyclotomic quotients. Our categories
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
and
\mathbf{Web}^{\Lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}
can alternately be viewed as a
thickening
of these objects. In particular, Savage’s constructions live inside these categories as thin-strand subcategories, see
Sections

10.7
and
12.1
.

In independent work, Song–W. Wang introduce the affine web category and affine Schur category in
[
30
,
31
]
and study their relation to cyclotomic Schur algebras and finite W-algebras. Their starting point is the same as ours in the special case
A=\mathbbm{k}
, but we have different goals in mind. For example, they only give the (skew-symmetric) defining representation under the assumption that
\mathbbm{k}
is a field; conversely, we do not consider connections to finite
W
-algebras. Shen–Song–W. Wang extend some of these results to the quantum setting in
[
28
]
. Likewise, generalizing work from
[
2
,
3
]
, Song–X. Wang independently introduce type
Q
affine webs in
[
32
]
which corresponds to the current paper when
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{1}
, the Clifford superalgebra on one generator. On a related front, in the forthcoming work
[
6
]
, Brundan-Ivanov study diagrammatics for the degenerate affine Schur category modified to incorporate symmetric polynomials on thick strands, and study the diagrammatic image of the Yangian associated to
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(\mathbbm{k})
.
Other related works appear in
[
7
,
23
,
25
]
, see below.

1.6.
Further directions

This paper establishes the foundations of affine
A
-webs and their cyclotomic qoutients, and sets the stage for a number of areas of research.

As discussed above, finite webs allow for a diagrammatic description of algebras which are Morita equivalent to the RoCK blocks of the symmetric groups and (conjecturally) related structures in positive characteristic. This paper is part of a program to prove these conjectures as well as suitably modified versions at affine and higher cyclotomic levels. It is worth mentioning that the generators-and-relations presentation and
\mathbbm{k}
-bases for
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
and its cyclotomic quotients established here will be an essential ingredient in that work. In particular, we propose the following, which generalizes the Morita equivalence of
[
17
, Corollary 6.17]
to the arbitrary characteristic setting.

Conjecture 1.6.1
.

Let
{\tt X}\in\{{\tt A}_{n},{\tt D}_{n},{\tt E}_{6,7,8}\}
, and take
\mathcal{A}
to be the data of the zigzag algebra
\bar{Z}({\tt X})
as described in
Section

2.2.3
. Then the affine web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
is equivalent to the category
\bigoplus_{d=0}^{\infty}C_{d\delta}\textup{-mod}
of finitely-generated
imaginary KLR
modules in affine type
{\tt X}^{(1)}
(see
[
17
, §2.6]
).

Work related to
1.6.1
has appeared elsewhere in the literature. The case
{\tt A}_{1}
was solved in
[
25
]
, and we expect our
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
category should be connected to the
curve Schur algebras

\mathcal{S}^{\mathbb{P}^{1}}_{n}
defined therein when one takes
A=\mathbbm{k}[x]/(x^{2})
,
\mathfrak{a}=\mathbbm{k}
. In
[
23
]
, the authors have defined
coil Schur algebras
which also conjecturally describe imaginary KLR strata—we expect that (for certain parameter choices), our
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
provides a diagrammatic, generators-and-relations presentation for their algebras up to Morita equivalence (see
[
23
, Conjecture 8.3, Remark 6.11]
). It would be interesting to fully delineate the connections to all the objects above.

An integral codeterminant basis is presented for finite webs for
A=\mathbbm{k}
in
[
5
]
. See
[
11
]
for a similar basis. These bases, in particular, show these categories have the structure of an object-adapted cellular category as defined in
[
10
]
. In light of the results of
[
20
]
— where it is shown that if
A
is based quasi-hereditary, then
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})}(n,d)
is again based quasi-hereditary via a generalized codeterminant basis — it is natural to speculate that the bases of
[
5
,
11
]
should generalize to
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
and its cyclotomic quotients when
\mathcal{A}
is based quasi-hereditary.

When
A
is Frobenius, one can also define oriented webs. This would be a thick version of the Heisenberg category studied in
[
7
]
. As the authors discuss in Remark 10.8 of
loc. cit.
, such a thick calculus could be helpful in computing Grothendieck rings when the base ring is an integral domain. Another interesting problem would be to define quantized affine Frobenius webs using the quantum wreath products from
[
24
]
.

2.
Frobenius superalgebras

2.1.
Frobenius great pairs

Let
\mathbbm{k}
be an characteristic zero domain viewed as an associative superalgebra concentrated in parity
\bar{0}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}=\mathbbm{Z}/2\mathbbm{Z}
. Let
\mathbbm{K}
be the field of fractions for
\mathbbm{k}
, also viewed as a superalgebra concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
. Unless otherwise noted, unlabelled tensor products of
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules are over
\mathbbm{k}
:
M\otimes N=M\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}N
.

The prefix “super” indicates a
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading and that signs are introduced according to the “sign rule” for graded objects. We often leave the prefix “super” implicit. We assume the reader is familiar with the basics of (locally unital) associative
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebras, supermodules, supermodule homomorphisms, (monoidal) supercategories, supernatural transformations, etc., and only remark as needed to set our notations and conventions.

2.1.1.
Frobenius superalgebras

Let
A=A_{\bar{0}}\oplus A_{\bar{1}}
be a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra with distinguished idempotent set
I\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
. In particular,
A=\oplus_{i,j\in I}jAi
. By definition, a basis for a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A
will be a homogeneous
\mathbbm{k}
-basis
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
for
jAi
, for all
i,j\in I
. We say
A
is
locally finite
if
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
is a finite set for all
i,j\in I
. Unless stated otherwise, all locally unital superalgebras will be assumed to be locally finite. Write
\mathtt{B}=\sqcup_{i,j\in I}({}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i})
. Write
\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}
,
\mathtt{B}_{\bar{1}}
for the even and odd elements of
\mathtt{B}
, respectively. For
k\in I
write
{}_{k}\mathtt{B}
for
\sqcup_{i}\left({}_{k}\mathtt{B}_{i}\right)
and write
\mathtt{B}_{k}
for
\sqcup_{j}\left({}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{k}\right)
.

By definition, an automorphism of a locally unital superalgebra
A
is an even superalgebra isomorphism
\eta:A\rightarrow A
that fixes the distinguished idempotents of
A
. For such an automorphism
\eta
and a right
A
-module
M
, we define the right
\eta
-twisted
module
M^{\eta}
to be
M
as a
\mathbbm{k}
-module, with
A
-action given by
m\cdot f=m\eta(f)
for all
f\in A
and
m\in M
. Likewise, for a left
A
-module
M
define the left
\eta
-twisted
module
{}^{\eta}M
via the
A
-action given by
f\cdot m=\eta(f)m
.

Let
A
be a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra and let
A^{*}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}(jAi)^{*}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}{\rm Hom}_{\mathbbm{k}}(jAi,\mathbbm{k})
denote the (local) dual. Consider
A^{*}
as an
A
-bimodule via

(2.1.1)

(f\cdot\theta\cdot g)(h):=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{\theta}+\bar{f}\bar{g}+\bar{f}\bar{h}}\theta(ghf),

for homogneous
\theta\in A^{*}
and homogeneous
f,g,h\in A
. Using this formula it is an easy calculation to show
j(A^{*})i=(iAj)^{*}
for all
i,j\in I
.

Here and below, when given a homogeneous element
m
of a
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule
M=M_{\bar{0}}\oplus M_{\bar{1}}
, we write
\overline{m}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
for the parity of
m
. Note, too, that we often give a formula only on homogeneous elements and leave it understood that the general case is given by linearity.

Definition 2.1.1
.

If a locally unital superalgebra
A
admits an even
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
\mathrm{tr}:A\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}
and an automorphism
\psi:A\rightarrow A
of locally unital superalgebras such that the map

(2.1.2)

\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}:A\rightarrow{}^{\psi}\left(A^{*}\right),\quad f\mapsto\left(\phi_{tr}(f):g\mapsto\mathrm{tr}(fg)\right).

is a parity preserving
A
-bimodule isomorphism,
then we say the data
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
makes
A
a
Frobenius superalgebra
.

For a Frobenius superalgebra, we call
\mathrm{tr}
the
trace map
and
\psi
the
Nakayama automorphism
. For brevity in upcoming formulas, write
{}_{t}a
for
\psi^{-t}(a)
for all
t\in\mathbbm{Z}
and
a\in A
.

A straightforward check verifies that
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
makes
A
a Frobenius superalgebra if and only if the map
\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}:=\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}\circ\psi^{-1}
given by

\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}:A\rightarrow\left(A^{*}\right)^{\psi^{-1}},\qquad f\mapsto(\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(f):g\mapsto(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\mathrm{tr}(gf)).

is an
A
-bimodule isomorphism. Our definition of Frobenius superalgebra is an extension of the definition used in
[
27
]
to the locally unital setting. Many of the basic results about these algebras can be found there. For example, the following result is standard.

Lemma 2.1.2
.

Say
A
is a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra such that
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius superalgebra. Then,

\mathrm{tr}\left(fg\right)=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\mathrm{tr}\left(g\psi(f)\right)=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\mathrm{tr}\left(\psi^{-1}(g)f\right),

for homogeneous
f,g\in A
.

2.1.2.
Results on Frobenius superalgebras

Assume
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra. Let
\mathtt{B}
be a basis for
A
. Then
A^{*}
has a dual basis
\{b^{*}\mid b\in\mathtt{B}\}
defined by
b^{*}(c)=\delta_{b,c}
for all
b,c\in\mathtt{B}
. Here
\delta_{b,c}
is the Kronecker delta function; more generally, if
P
is a proposition, then we write
\delta_{P}
for the function that is
1
if
P
is true, and
0
if
P
is false.

If

b^{\vee}:=\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}(b^{*})

for all
b\in\mathtt{B}
, then the set
\mathtt{B}^{\vee}=\{b^{\vee}\mid b\in\mathtt{B}\}
forms a homogeneous basis for
A
satisfying
\mathrm{tr}(b^{\vee}c)=\delta_{b,c}
for all
b,c\in\mathtt{B}
. We call
\mathtt{B}^{\vee}
the
(left) dual basis
for
A
.

Note that the operation
c\mapsto c^{\vee}
is dependent on the choice of a basis. We sometimes leave this choice implicit. For example, when we write
(b^{\vee})^{\vee}
in the next lemma and later, this should be understood as the dual of
b^{\vee}
with respect to the basis
\mathtt{B}^{\vee}
. That is, it is the element of
A
determined by
\mathrm{tr}\left(\left((b^{\vee})^{\vee}\right)\left(c^{\vee}\right)\right)=\delta_{b^{\vee},c^{\vee}}=\delta_{b,c}
for all
c\in\mathtt{B}
.

The following properties are straightforward to check.

Lemma 2.1.3
.

Let
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a Frobenius superalgebra with basis
\mathtt{B}
. The following statements are true.

(1)

The trace function satisfies

\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}(jAi)=\begin{cases}\mathbbm{k}&\textup{if }j=i;\\
0&\textup{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(2)

The map
\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}
restricts to a linear isomorphism
\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}:jAi\xrightarrow{\sim}(iAj)^{*}
for all
i,j\in I
.

(3)

The set
({}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i})^{\vee}=\{b^{\vee}\mid b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\}
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
iAj
.

(4)

If
I\subseteq\mathtt{B}
, then for all
b\in\mathtt{B}
,
\mathrm{tr}(b^{\vee})=\delta_{b\in I}
.

(5)

For all
b\in\mathtt{B}
,
(b^{\vee})^{\vee}=(-1)^{\bar{b}}\psi^{-1}(b)
.

(6)

For all
b\in\mathtt{B}
,
\psi(b^{\vee})=\psi(b)^{\vee}
, where
\psi(b)^{\vee}
is the dual of
\psi(b)
defined using the basis
\left\{\psi(b)\mid b\in\mathtt{B}\right\}
.

2.1.3.
Good pairs and Frobenius great pairs

Definition 2.1.4
.

Let
I\subseteq\mathfrak{a}\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
be an even subalgebra of
A
that contains
I
, the set of distinguished idempotents. We say that
\mathcal{A}=(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
is a
good pair
provided there exists a basis
\mathtt{B}
for
A
such that
{}_{j}\mathtt{b}_{i}:={}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\cap\mathfrak{a}
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
j\mathfrak{a}i
, and
i\in{}_{i}\mathtt{b}_{i}
for all
i\in I
.

We call a basis of
A
a
good basis
if it satisfies the above definition. If
\mathcal{A}=(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
is a good pair we will usually choose to use a good basis for
A
. However, we will occasionally need to make use of other bases. For example, if
\mathtt{B}
is a good basis, then
\mathtt{B}^{\vee}
may fail to be a good basis.

Definition 2.1.5
.

We say that the data
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a
Frobenius good pair
provided that
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
is a good pair,
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a locally unital Frobenius superalgebra, and the Nakayama automorphism restricts to an automorphism of
\mathfrak{a}
.

Let
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a Frobenius good pair. Let
\left(A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})\right)^{*}\xrightarrow{\pi^{*}}A^{*}
be the dual of the canonical projection map
\pi:A\rightarrow A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})
.

Lemma 2.1.6
.

Let
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a Frobenius good pair. Then the following are equivalent:

(1)

There exists a good basis
\mathtt{B}
with the property that
b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a}
for all
b\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}
.

(2)

The
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map

(2.1.3)

\left(A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})\right)^{*}\xrightarrow{\pi^{*}}A^{*}\xrightarrow{\phi^{-1}_{\mathrm{tr}}}A

has image contained in
\mathfrak{a}
.

(3)

Every good basis
\mathtt{B}
has the property that
b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a}
for all
b\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}
.

Proof.

We first prove
(1)
implies
(2)
. Say
\mathtt{B}
is a good basis that satisfies the property in
(1)
. Since
\left\{\pi(c)\mid c\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}\right\}
is a basis for
A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})
, a basis for
\left(A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})\right)^{*}
is given by
\left\{\pi(b)^{*}\mid b\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}\right\}
, where
\pi(b)^{*}
is defined by declaring
\pi(b)^{*}(\pi(c))=\delta_{b,c}
for all
c\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}
.
The linear functional
\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*})\in A^{*}
evaluates on
c\in\mathtt{B}
by

\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*})(c)=\pi(b)^{*}(\pi(c))=\delta_{b,c}.

In other words,
\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*})=b^{*}
as linear functionals on
A
. By the definition of
b^{\vee}
,
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}\left(\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*})\right)=\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}\left(b^{*}\right)=b^{\vee}
, which is an element of
\mathfrak{a}
by assumption. Thus, we have found a basis of
\left(A/(A_{\bar{1}}+\mathfrak{a})\right)^{*}
whose image under
\phi^{-1}_{\mathrm{tr}}\circ\pi^{*}
is contained in
\mathfrak{a}
, establishing the desired containment in (2).

We next prove that
(2)
implies
(3)
. Let
b\in\mathtt{B}_{\bar{0}}\setminus\mathtt{b}_{\bar{0}}
. Using the notation of the previous paragraph and the definition of
b^{\vee}
,
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(b^{\vee})=b^{*}=\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*})
and so
b^{\vee}=\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}(\pi^{*}(\pi(b)^{*}))
is in
\mathfrak{a}
, as desired.

It is immediate that
(3)
implies
(1)
.
∎

Definition 2.1.7
.

We say that the data
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius
great
pair (or simply that
\mathcal{A}
is
great
) if it is a Frobenius good pair and if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of
Lemma

2.1.6
.

Unless otherwise stated, going forward we will assume that
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius great pair. To better understand the role of these assumptions, see
Section

2.2
for examples and
Section

2.3
for further discussion.

2.2.
Examples

2.2.1.
A=\mathbbm{k}
and other Frobenius superalgebras

Let
A=\mathfrak{a}=\mathbbm{k}
, let
I=\{1\}
, let
\mathrm{tr}:A\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}
be the identity map, and let
\psi:A\rightarrow A
be the identity map. Then
\mathcal{A}=((\mathbbm{k},\mathbbm{k})_{\{1\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is trivially a Frobenius great pair.

More generally, let
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a locally unital Frobenius superalgebra with distinguished idempotents
I
. If
A
admits a homogeneous basis
\mathtt{B}
for
A
that contains
I
, then
(A,A_{\bar{0}})_{I}
is a good pair. Furthermore,
((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is trivially a Frobenius great pair. In particular, since a locally unital Frobenius algebra
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
with distinguished idempotents
I
can always be viewed as a superalgebra concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
, it follows that
((A,A)_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is always a Frobenius great pair if it admits a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis that contains
I
.

If
A=\mathbbm{k}G
is the group ring of a finite group
G
with identity element
e_{G}\in G
, then it is well-known that taking
\mathrm{tr}(g)=\delta_{e_{G},g}
and
\psi(g)=g
for all
g\in G
makes
A
into a Frobenius superalgebra concentrated in parity
\bar{0}
. If
H
is a proper subgroup of
G
, then
((\mathbbm{k}G,\mathbbm{k}H)_{\{e_{G}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius good pair but is never great.

If
A=\mathbbm{k}[x]/(x^{m})
is a truncated polynomial algebra for some
m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
, then
A=A_{\bar{0}}
is symmetric Frobenius with trace map given by
\mathrm{tr}(x^{t})=\delta_{t,m-1}
. If
\mathfrak{a}=A
then
\mathcal{A}=((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi))
is a Frobenius great pair by the above discussion. One other interesting option for a Frobenius great pair is the case
\mathfrak{a}=\mathbbm{k}\langle x^{2}\rangle
when
m
is even.

The next example is a locally unital version of Laurent polynomials. Let
\mathcal{C}
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear category with set of objects equal to the integers and with
{\rm Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,b)=\mathbbm{k}T_{b,a}
, where, by definition,
T_{c,b}\circ T_{b,a}=T_{c,a}
for all
a,b,c\in\mathbbm{Z}
. Let
A=\oplus_{a,b\in\mathbbm{Z}}{\rm Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,b)=\oplus_{a,b\in\mathbbm{Z}}\mathbbm{k}T_{b,a}
be the path algebra. This can be made into a superalgebra by declaring
\overline{T}_{b,a}=\overline{b-a}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
. Let
\mathfrak{a}
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-span of
\left\{T_{b,a}\mid\overline{b-a}=\bar{0},\text{ and }b\geq a\right\}
and let
I=\left\{T_{a,a}\mid a\in\mathbbm{Z}\right\}
. Define
\mathrm{tr}:A\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}
by
\mathrm{tr}(T_{b,a})=\delta_{a,b}
, and
\psi:A\rightarrow A
be the identity map. Then both
\left((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
and
\left((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
are Frobenius great pairs.

2.2.2.
Clifford and Grassmann superalgebras

Let
A=\operatorname{Cl}_{t}=\mathbbm{k}[c_{1},\dotsc,c_{t}]/(\{c_{i}c_{j}=-c_{j}c_{i},c_{i}^{2}=1\mid 1\leq i\neq j\leq t\})
be the Clifford superalgebra on
t
generators with
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading given by declaring
\bar{c_{i}}=\bar{1}
for
i=1,\dotsc,t
. Then
A
has
\mathbbm{k}
-basis given by
\mathtt{B}=\left\{c_{1}^{r_{1}}\dotsb c_{t}^{r_{t}}\mid r_{k}\in\left\{0,1\right\}\right\}
. Set
I=\{1_{A}\}
. Let
\mathrm{tr}:A\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}
be given by

\mathrm{tr}(c_{1}^{r_{1}}\dotsb c_{t}^{r_{t}})=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }r_{1}=\dotsb=r_{t}=0;\\
0&\text{ otherwise,}\par\end{cases}

and let
\psi:A\rightarrow A
be given by
\psi(x)=(-1)^{\bar{x}}x
. Then, both
((A,\mathbbm{k}1_{A})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
and
((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
are good Frobenius pairs, but only
((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius great pair when
t>1
.

Now let
A=\Lambda_{t}=\mathbbm{k}[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{t}]/(\{x_{i}x_{j}=-x_{j}x_{i},x_{i}^{2}=0\mid 1\leq i\neq j\leq t\})
be the Grassmann superalgebra on
t
generators with
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading given by declaring
\bar{x_{i}}=\bar{1}
for
i=1,\dotsc,t
. Then
A
has
\mathbbm{k}
-basis given by
\mathtt{B}=\left\{x_{1}^{r_{1}}\dotsb x_{t}^{r_{t}}\mid r_{k}\in\left\{0,1\right\}\right\}
. Set
I=\{1_{A}\}
. Let
\mathrm{tr}:A\rightarrow\mathbbm{k}
be given by

\mathrm{tr}(x_{1}^{r_{1}}\dotsb x_{t}^{r_{t}})=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }r_{1}=\dotsb=r_{t}=1;\\
0&\text{ otherwise,}\par\end{cases}

and let
\psi:A\rightarrow A
be given by
\psi(x)=(-1)^{\bar{x}}x
. In order for
\mathrm{tr}
to be an even map, let us assume
t=2p
for some
p>0
. Let
\mathfrak{a}
be the
\mathbbm{k}
-span of
1_{A}
and all even basis elements that satisfy
\sum_{i=1}^{t}r_{i}\geq p
. Then
\mathfrak{a}
is easily seen to be a subalgebra of
A_{\bar{0}}
. A direct check verifies that
((A,\mathbbm{k}1_{A})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
,
((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
, and
((A,\mathfrak{a})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
are Frobenius good pairs, but only
((A,A_{\bar{0}})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
and
((A,\mathfrak{a})_{\{1_{A}\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
are Frobenius great pairs

2.2.3.
Zigzag superalgebras

Let
\Gamma=(I,E)
be a simple connected graph with no loops. For each pair of connected vertices
i\textup{\textemdash}j
, fix
\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{ji}\in\{\pm 1\}
. Then the associated locally unital
zigzag superalgebra

\overline{Z}(\Gamma)=\overline{Z}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}j\overline{Z}i
has distinguished set of orthogonal idempotents corresponding to the vertices
I
of
\Gamma
, with the following
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for each subspace:

\displaystyle j\overline{Z}i=\begin{cases}\mathbbm{k}\{i,c_{i}\}&\textup{if }i=j;\\
\mathbbm{k}\{a_{ji}\}&\textup{if }i\textup{\textemdash}j;\\
0&\textup{otherwise},\end{cases}

Multiplication is defined via the orthogonality of the idempotents
I
, coupled with the additional rules:

\displaystyle a_{kj}a_{ji}=\delta_{ik}\varepsilon_{ji}c_{i},\qquad c_{i}a_{ij}=a_{ij}c_{j}=0,\qquad c_{i}^{2}=0.

The parity of elements is defined by
\bar{i}=\bar{c}_{i}=\bar{0}
,
\bar{a}_{ij}=\bar{1}
.
Taking
\mathrm{tr}(i)=\mathrm{tr}(a_{ji})=0
,
\mathrm{tr}(c_{i})=1
for all
i,j\in I
, and
\psi(a_{ji})=-\varepsilon_{ij}\varepsilon_{ji}a_{ji}
, it is straightforward to verify that
((\bar{Z},\mathbbm{k}I)_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
is a Frobenius great pair.

2.2.4.
Trivial extension superalgebras

The trivial extension algebra is a well-known technique for turning a finite-dimensional associative algebra into a Frobenius algebra. Suitably modified, this machine also applies here.

Let
C
be a locally finite, locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra and let
C^{*}
be the dual viewed as a bimodule via
Eq.

2.1.1
. Set

E(C)=C^{*}\oplus C

as a
\mathbbm{k}
-module. The
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading is given by declaring
E(C)_{r}=(C^{*}_{r},C_{r})
for
r\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
. In particular, this implies
\overline{(\alpha,a)}=\overline{\alpha}=\overline{a}
. Define the product by

(\alpha,a)\cdot(\beta,b)=(\alpha\cdot b+a\cdot\beta,ab).

This makes
E(C)
into a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra, where
C
is identified as a subsuperalgebra of
E(C)
in the obvious way. In particular,
I\subseteq C\subseteq E(C)
provides a set of distinguished idempotents. Moreover,
jE(C)i=j\cdot(C^{*})\cdot i\oplus jCi=(iCj)^{*}\oplus jCi
for all
i,j\in I
, and
E(C)=\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}jE(C)i
.

If
\mathtt{C}
is a homogenous basis for
C
,
c^{*}\in C^{*}
is defined by
c^{*}(d)=\delta_{c,d}
for all
d\in\mathtt{C}
, and if we set
\mathtt{C}^{*}=\left\{c^{*}\mid c\in\mathtt{C}\right\}
, then the basis
\mathtt{B}=\left\{(c^{*},0),(0,c)\mid c\in\mathtt{C}\right\}
makes
(E(C),C_{\bar{0}})_{I}
a good pair. Define a trace map by

\mathrm{tr}:E(C)\rightarrow\mathbbm{k},\quad\mathrm{tr}(\alpha,a)=\sum_{i\in I}\alpha(i),

and let the Nakayama automorphism
\psi:E(C)\rightarrow E(C)
be the identity map. We claim the data
\left((E(C),C_{\bar{0}})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
is a Frobenius great pair.

Consider the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}:E(C)\rightarrow E(C)^{*}
defined by the trace map as in
Eq.

2.1.2
. We claim this map is a
k
-linear isomorphism. Note that for homogeneous
(\alpha,a),(\beta,b)\in E(c)
one has

\left[\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\alpha,a)\right](\beta,b)=\mathrm{tr}((\alpha,a)(\beta,b))=\mathrm{tr}(\alpha\cdot b+a\cdot\beta,ab)=\alpha(b)+(-1)^{\bar{a}\bar{\beta}}\beta(a).

Let
c,d\in\mathtt{C}
. The previous calculation verifies that

\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(c^{*},0)(0,d)

\displaystyle=c^{*}(d)=\delta_{c,d},

\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(c^{*},0)(d^{*},0)

\displaystyle=0,

\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(0,c)(0,d)

\displaystyle=0,

\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(0,c)(d^{*},0)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\bar{c}\bar{d}}d^{*}(c)=(-1)^{\bar{c}}\delta_{c,d}.

That is,
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(c^{*},0)=(0,c)^{*}
and
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(0,c)=(-1)^{\bar{c}}(c^{*},0)^{*}
. Thus,
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}
defines a homogeneous bijection between
\mathbbm{k}
-bases of
E(C)
and
E(C)^{*}
and, hence, defines an isomorphism of
\mathbbm{k}
-modules. Moreover, this calculation shows that
(c^{*},0)^{\vee}=\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}\left((c^{*},0)^{*}\right)=(0,c)\in C_{\bar{0}}
for
c\in\mathtt{C}_{\bar{0}}
and so the data
\left((E(C),C_{\bar{0}})_{\{1\}},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
satisfies the great condition.

We next claim that
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}
is a morphism of
(E(C),E(C))
-bimodules. Let
(\alpha,a)
,
(\beta,b)
, and
(\gamma,g)
be homogenous elements of
E(C)
. Then

\displaystyle\left((\alpha,a)\cdot\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\beta,b)\right)(\gamma,g)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\overline{(\alpha,a)}(\overline{(\beta,b)}+\overline{(\gamma,g)})}\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\beta,b)((\gamma,g)(\alpha,a))

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\overline{a}(\overline{b}+\overline{g})}\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\beta,b)((\gamma\cdot a+g\cdot\alpha,ga))

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\overline{a}(\overline{b}+\overline{g})}\mathrm{tr}\left((\beta,b)(\gamma\cdot a+g\cdot\alpha,ga)\right)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\overline{a}(\overline{b}+\overline{g})}\mathrm{tr}\left(\beta\cdot ga+b\cdot\gamma\cdot a+bg\cdot\alpha,bga)\right)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\overline{a}(\overline{b}+\overline{g})}\left(\beta(ga)+(-1)^{\bar{b}(\bar{g}+\bar{a})}\gamma(ab)+(-1)^{(\bar{b}+\bar{g})\bar{\alpha}}\alpha(bg)\right),

whereas,

\displaystyle\left(\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}((\alpha,a)(\beta,b)\right)(\gamma,g)

\displaystyle=\left(\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\alpha\cdot b+a\cdot\beta,ab)\right)(\gamma,g)

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}\left((\alpha\cdot b+a\cdot\beta,ab)(\gamma,g)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}\left(\alpha\cdot bg+ab\cdot\gamma+a\cdot\beta\cdot g,abg\right)

\displaystyle=\alpha(bg)+(-1)^{(\bar{a}+\bar{b})\bar{g}}\gamma(ab)+(-1)^{\bar{a}(\bar{b}+\bar{g})}\beta(ga).

Thus
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}
is a homomorphism of left
E(C)
-modules.

On the other hand,

\left(\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\beta,b)\cdot(\alpha,a)\right)(\gamma,g)=\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}(\beta,b)\left((\alpha,a)(\gamma,g)\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left((\beta,b)(\alpha,a)(\gamma,g)\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left((\beta,b)(\alpha,a)\right)(\gamma,g).

Thus
\phi_{\mathrm{tr}}
is a homomorphism of right
E(C)
-modules. This verifies that
\left((E(C),C_{\bar{0}})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
is a Frobenius great pair.

2.3.
A discussion of assumptions

Our assumptions on
\mathbbm{k}
and
\mathcal{A}=((A,a)_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
were selected to include the examples and applications of interest to the authors. The reader may wish to make different assumptions. In this section we briefly discuss how toggling on/off various assumptions affects the results of the paper.

2.3.1.
Ground ring

The reader may prefer to work with a ground field of characteristic zero. If so, then the affine web category for any choice of
\mathfrak{a}\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
is isomorphic to the one obtained by selecting
\mathfrak{a}=A_{\bar{0}}
, in which case the Frobenius great pair requirements are trivially satisfied. Likewise, cyclotomic datum are automatically regular (see
Section

12
). Thus the results of this paper hold unconditionally for any locally unital Frobenius superalgebra when working over a field of characteristic zero. Moreover, a number of the definitions and proofs can be simplified.

2.3.2.
Locally finite, locally unital Frobenius superalgebras

Readers who are not interested in
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-gradings may assume that
A
is an associative
\mathbbm{k}
-algebra. One can view
A
as a superalgebra concentrated in parity
0
by declaring
A=A_{\bar{0}}\oplus A_{\bar{1}}=A\oplus 0
. The results of this paper apply with the simplification that all signs due to
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-gradings disappear.

Associative superalgebras frequently come with a distinguished set of idempotents. For example, if the superalgebra is defined as the quotient of the path superalgebra of some quiver (e.g., see the zigzag superalgebras and
[
29
, Section IV.16]
). Another important example is if
\mathcal{C}
is a small category enriched over the category of free
k
-supermodules with a fixed set of isomorphism classes of objects,
X
. The associated path algebra,

\bigoplus_{x,y\in X}{\rm Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(x,y),

is naturally a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra with
I=\left\{{\rm Id}_{x}\mid x\in X\right\}
the set of distinguished idempotents.

The Frobenius property
Eq.

2.1.2
forces
A
to satisfy a suitable finiteness property. When
A
is unital, a Frobenius structure forces
A
to have finite rank. If
A
is locally unital, then local finiteness is the appropriate choice (see (2) of
Lemma

2.1.3
). By allowing locally unital superalgebras, our framework allows for examples that have infinite total rank like the one in
Section

2.2.1
. Another important advantage of including a set of distinguished idempotents is that it allows for greater refinement in the definitions and results.

The reader who prefers their associative superalgebras to be unital may choose
I=\left\{1_{A}\right\}
. The results of this paper simplify in that strands in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
have a single color (and, hence, are determined by their thickness), the crossing generators in
Eq.

5.1.1
are omitted, and the relations
Eqs.

3.2.5
,
3.2.6
, and
3.2.7
are omitted.

For simplicity’s sake this paper assumes the Nakayama automorphism fixes the distinguished idempotents. The results of this paper go through with appropriate modifications as long as the Nakayama automorphism fixes the distinguished idempotents as a set. In that case, for example, the affine dot would define a morphism in
{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(i,\psi^{-1}(i))
for each
i\in I
. Fearing most readers would find the associated bookkeeping a journey into madness (and, indeed, the authors spent some time on this particular journey), we forgo that extra level of generality.

Likewise, while we choose not to do so, it would be interesting to allow the trace map to be odd. This odd trace map occurs, for example, when studying Frobenius structures on odd rank Grassman superalgebras, or by modifying the Frobenius structure on odd rank Clifford algebras that we described in the previous section. We expect the results of this paper to generalize with suitable modifications (e.g., odd Casimir elements in
A\otimes A
and odd affine dots in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
) along with additional signs that would need to be tracked.

2.3.3.
Frobenius great pairs

The Frobenius structure on
A
is essential for defining the Casimir elements, the affine dot (e.g., see
Eq.

5.1.3
), and the action of the affine dot on
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules (e.g., see
Proposition

9.2.1
). The even subalgebra
\mathfrak{a}\subseteq A_{\bar{0}}
and the notion of a good pair
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
is needed if we wish to define
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
integrally (i.e., over the integral domain
\mathbbm{k}
). Different choices of
\mathfrak{a}
can be viewed as making different choices of
\mathbbm{k}
-form inside the
\mathbbm{K}
-linear category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}}
defined using the superalgebra
\mathbbm{K}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}A
. It is known that the choice of good pair
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
dramatically affects the representation theory of the superalgebras
T_{(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}}(n,d)
obtained from the Schurification of
(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}

[
19
]
. We expect the choice of good pair to be influential here, as well.

Likewise, the fact we wish to work integrally motivates the assumption that
\mathcal{A}
is a Frobenius great pair. Specifically, the great condition ensures the coefficients which appear in relation
Eq.

5.1.3
lie in
\mathbbm{k}
.

2.4.
Casimir elements in a Frobenius superalgebra

Let
(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a locally unital Frobenius superalgebra. Let
M
be a left
A
-module,
N
be a right
A
-module, and let
\eta
be an automorphism of
A
. Then there is a natural isomorphism of
(A,A)
-bimodules:

(2.4.1)

\displaystyle D_{\eta}:N^{*}\otimes(M^{*})^{\eta}\rightarrow((M\otimes N)^{*})^{\eta},\qquad\beta\otimes\alpha\mapsto((x\otimes y)\mapsto(-1)^{\bar{\beta}\bar{\alpha}+\bar{\beta}\bar{x}}\alpha(x)\beta(y)

For
i\in I
, define
m_{i}:Ai\otimes iA\rightarrow A
as the restriction of the multiplication map on
A
. Then we define an
(A,A)
-bimodule homomorphism

\displaystyle\Delta_{i}:A\rightarrow Ai\otimes iA

as the composition

A\xrightarrow{\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}}(A^{*})^{\psi^{-1}}\xrightarrow{m_{i}^{*}}(Ai\otimes iA)^{*})^{\psi^{-1}}\xrightarrow{D_{\psi^{-1}}^{-1}}(iA)^{*}\otimes((Ai)^{*})^{\psi^{-1}}\xrightarrow{\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}\otimes\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}^{-1}}Ai\otimes iA,

where
D_{\psi^{-1}}
is given by
Eq.

2.4.1
.

Lemma 2.4.1
.

Let
i,j\in I
. Then,
\Delta_{i}(j)=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}
.

Proof.

Let
u,v\in\mathtt{B}_{i}
. Set
x=(u^{\vee})^{\vee}
,
y=v^{\vee}
. By Lemma
2.1.3
(3), such elements
x,y
comprise bases for the spaces
Ai
and
iA
respectively. We have

\displaystyle(m_{j,i}^{*}\circ\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(j))(x\otimes y)

\displaystyle=\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(j)(xy)=\mathrm{tr}(xyj)=\delta_{y\in Aj}\mathrm{tr}(xy)=\delta_{v\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\mathrm{tr}((u^{\vee})^{\vee}v^{\vee})=\delta_{v\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\delta_{u,v}.

On the other hand,

\displaystyle\left((D_{\psi^{-1}}\circ\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}\otimes\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)\right)(x\otimes y)

\displaystyle=D_{\psi^{-1}}\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(b)\otimes\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(b^{\vee})\right)(x\otimes y)

\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}(-1)^{\bar{b}+\bar{b}\bar{x}}\mathrm{tr}(xb^{\vee})\mathrm{tr}(yb)

\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}(-1)^{\bar{b}+\bar{b}\bar{u}}\mathrm{tr}((u^{\vee})^{\vee}b^{\vee})\mathrm{tr}(v^{\vee}b)

\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}(-1)^{\bar{b}+\bar{b}\bar{u}}\delta_{u,b}\delta_{v,b}=\delta_{v\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\delta_{u,v}.

Thus
m_{j,i}^{*}\circ\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}(j)=D\circ\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}\otimes\varphi_{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)
. The result then follows from the definition of
\Delta_{i}
.
∎

It follows that elements of the form
\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}
are independent of the choice of basis
\mathtt{B}
. In particular, for any
i,j\in I
, we can replace the basis
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
for
jAi
with the basis
({}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j})^{\vee}=\{b^{\vee}\mid b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}\}
, which implies

(2.4.2)

\displaystyle\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}=\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}b^{\vee}\otimes(b^{\vee})^{\vee}.

We call these the
(local) Casimir elements
of
A\otimes A
.

Let
\tau:A\otimes A\rightarrow A\otimes A
be the signed flip map
x\otimes y\mapsto(-1)^{\bar{x}\bar{y}}y\otimes x
.

Lemma 2.4.2
.

For all
i,j\in I
, we have
\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}
.

Proof.

The result follows from a direct calculation:

\displaystyle\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}b^{\vee}\otimes(b^{\vee})^{\vee}\right)=\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}(-1)^{\bar{b}}(b^{\vee})^{\vee}\otimes b^{\vee}\;\;=\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee},

where the first and last equalities follow from
Eq.

2.4.2
and
Lemma

2.1.3
(5), respectively.
∎

Given a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra
A
, the
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule
A\otimes A
is again a locally unital
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra with product given by
(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{\bar{g}\bar{x}}fx\otimes gy
.

Lemma 2.4.3
.

Let
f\in kAj
,
g\in\ell Ai
. Then the product on
A\otimes A
satisfies

(2.4.3)

\displaystyle(f\otimes g)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{k}\mathtt{B}_{\ell}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)(\psi(g)\otimes f).

and

(2.4.4)

\displaystyle(g\otimes f)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{g}}\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{\ell}\mathtt{B}_{k}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}\right)(f\otimes\psi(g)).

Proof.

First, recalling that
\Delta_{i}
is an
A
-bimodule map,

(2.4.5)

(f\otimes i)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=f\cdot\Delta_{i}(j)=\Delta_{i}(f)=\Delta_{i}(k)\cdot f=\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{k}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)(i\otimes f),

where the first and last equalities are from
Lemma

2.4.1
.
This identity along with use of the flip map yields:

\displaystyle(j\otimes g)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)

\displaystyle=\tau\left((g\otimes j)\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}g\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}\right)

\displaystyle=\tau(\psi^{-1}\otimes 1)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi(g)b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)

\displaystyle=\tau\left((\psi^{-1}\otimes 1)\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{\ell}\mathtt{B}_{j}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\psi(g)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{\ell}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}\psi(g)\right)

\displaystyle=\tau\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{\ell}\mathtt{B}_{j}}\psi^{-1}(b)\otimes b^{\vee}\right)\tau(j\otimes\psi(g))

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{\ell}}b\otimes b^{\vee}\right)(\psi(g)\otimes j).

Since
(f\otimes g)=(f\otimes\ell)(j\otimes g)
, this establishes
Eq.

2.4.3
. The second identity follows from applying
\tau
to both sides of
Eq.

2.4.3
and applying
Lemma

2.4.2
.
∎

3.
The finite web category
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}

We assume the reader is familar with constructing monoidal supercategories by generators and relations, diagrammatic supercategories, and the like. A recommended reference is
[
4
]
. This section summarizes needed definitions and results from
[
9
]
. Further details can be found in therein.

3.1.
Combinatorics

3.1.1.
Counting and sets

We use the generalized binomial coefficient:

\displaystyle\binom{n}{k}:=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}\in\mathbbm{Z},

for any
n\in\mathbbm{Z}
,
k\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Given integers
a,b
with
a\leq b
, let
[a,b]=\{a,a+1,\dotsc,b\}
. Given sets
X
and
Y
, we write
X^{Y}
for the set of tuples indexed by
Y
consisting of elements from
X
.

3.1.2.
Compositions

For
\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{t})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{t}
, set

\displaystyle|\mathbf{x}|=t,\qquad\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\sum_{k=1}^{t}x_{k},\qquad\mathbf{x}!=\prod_{k=1}^{t}(x_{k}!).

Set

\displaystyle\Omega(n,d)=\{\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=d\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Omega=\bigsqcup_{n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\Omega(n,d).

We also set

\displaystyle\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{x}}:=\mathfrak{S}_{x_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathfrak{S}_{x_{t}}\leq\mathfrak{S}_{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert}.

If
\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert
and
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{y}}\leq\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{x}}
, then we write
\mathscr{D}_{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathbf{y}}
for the set of minimal length right coset representatives for
\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{y}}\backslash\mathfrak{S}_{\mathbf{x}}
.

3.1.3.
Colored compositions

For
n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
and a set
I
, an
n
-part
I
-colored composition of
d
is the data of a composition
\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\Omega(n,d)
, and a tuple
\mathbf{i}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})\in I^{n}
, which we write as
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})
. For two such
I
-colored compositions, we declare
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{x})}
provided
i_{t}=j_{t}
whenever
x_{t}\neq 0
; i.e., the coloring of the zero components of a composition is irrelevant for us. Set

\displaystyle\Omega_{I}(n,d)=\{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})\mid\mathbf{i}\in I^{n},\,\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Omega_{I}=\bigsqcup_{n,d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}\Omega_{I}(n,d).

We consider
\Omega_{I}
as a monoid under concatenation, with identity the empty composition
()\in\Omega_{I}(0,0)
. We define the monoid of
reduced

I
-colored compositions
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
by imposing the following additional relation on
\Omega_{I}
:
()=(i^{(0)})
for all
i\in I
. In other words, we have
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}
in
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
provided the colored compositions are identical after deleting all the zero components. We write

\displaystyle\widehat{\Omega}_{I}(n,d)=\{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=(i_{1}^{(x_{1})},\ldots,i_{n}^{(x_{n})})\mid\mathbf{i}\in I^{n},\,\mathbf{x}\in\Omega(n,d)\}\subseteq\widehat{\Omega}_{I}.

For
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})}\in\widehat{\Omega}
, we will write
\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}}:=((i_{1}^{(1)})^{x_{1}},\ldots,(i_{t}^{(1)})^{x_{t}})\in\widehat{\Omega}
. We will also associate
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
with
\mathbf{i}^{(1^{n})}=(i_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,i_{n}^{(1)})\in\widehat{\Omega}
.

Example 3.1.1
.

If
I=\{\alpha,\beta\}
, then
\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}=\alpha^{(2)}\alpha^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}
in both
\Omega_{I}
and
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
, while
\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(0)}\beta^{(3)}=\alpha^{(2)}\beta^{(3)}
in
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
but not in
\Omega_{I}
.

3.2.
The
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
category

Let
\mathcal{A}=(A,\mathfrak{a})_{I}
be a good pair. It will be useful to set
A^{(1)}=A
and
A^{(z)}=\mathfrak{a}
for
z>1
.

Definition 3.2.1
.

Let
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
be the strict monoidal
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory defined as follows.
We have
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}})=\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
. The monoidal structure on objects in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
is inherited from the monoid
\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
; in particular the objects of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are monoidally generated by objects
i^{(x)}
for
i\in I
,
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, with
i^{(0)}
equating to the unit object
\mathbbm{1}\in\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
for all
i\in I
.

The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given by the diagrams:

i,j\in I
,
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
,
f\in jA^{(z)}i
, where diagrams are to be read from bottom to top. We call these morphisms
split
,
merge
,
crossing
, and
coupon
, respectively. Splits, merges and crossings have parity
\bar{0}
, and the parity of the
f
coupon is
\bar{f}
. We say a strand labeled by
i^{(x)}
has
color

i
and
thickness

x
. We refer to strands of thickness 1 as
thin
strands, otherwise we call them
thick
. Note that, since
A^{(1)}=A
and
A^{(z)}=\mathfrak{a}
for
z>1
, thick strands may only be decorated by coupons in the even subalgebra
\mathfrak{a}
, whereas thin strands may be decorated with arbitrary coupons in
A
.

Going forward, we will use the following conventions:

•

Strands of thickness
0
(and any coupons thereon) are to be deleted;

•

Diagrams containing a strand of negative thickness are to be read as zero.

•

When coupons on separate strands are depicted at the same height, the coupon on the left should be considered to be slightly above the coupon on the right.

\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given in
Eq.

3.2.2
-
Eq.

3.2.12
:

Web-associativity.

Lemma 3.3.2
.

The Coxeter, split- and merge-intertwining relations (
3.2.5
)–(
3.2.7
) hold in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
for any
i,j,k\in I
(not just distinct
i,j,k
).

in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(i^{(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n})},i^{(x_{1})}\cdots i^{(x_{n})})

and

\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(i^{(x_{1})}\cdots i^{(x_{n})},i^{(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n})})
, respectively. The diagrams should be interpreted as
n-1
vertically composed splits (or merges). By
Eq.

3.2.2
the resulting morphism is independent of the split (or merge) order.

For
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{t}^{(x_{t})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}})
recall that
\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}}=(i_{1}^{(1)})^{x_{1}}\cdots(i_{t}^{(1)})^{x_{t}}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}})
, and

\displaystyle Y_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle:=y_{i_{1}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes y_{i_{t}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\in\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}})

\displaystyle Z_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle:=z_{i_{1}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes z_{i_{t}}^{(1,\ldots,1)}\in\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})})

Then for
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}\in\textup{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}})
, we have linear maps:

\displaystyle exp_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{j}^{\mathbf{y}}),\qquad f\mapsto Y_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ f\circ Z_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

\displaystyle con_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{j}^{\mathbf{y}})\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}),\qquad f\mapsto Z_{\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ f\circ Y_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}}

We refer to these maps as
explosion
and
contraction
, respectively.
The next lemma follows by repeated application of
Eq.

3.2.4
.

Lemma 3.4.1
.

For all
f\in\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
, we have

\displaystyle con_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}\circ exp_{\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}}(f)=\mathbf{x}!\,\mathbf{y}!\,f.

For any
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
i_{1},\ldots,i_{x}\in I
, Lemma
3.3.2
implies there is a natural way to associate a permutation
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{x}
to a morphism in
{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\left(i_{1}^{(1)}\cdots i_{x}^{(1)},i_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}^{(1)}\cdots i_{\sigma^{-1}(x)}^{(1)}\right)
which associates simple transpositions with the appropriately colored crossing.

Lemma 3.4.2

For all

\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m}

\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert

for all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
.

Proof.

One may see this via a straightforward induction proof using relation (
3.2.3
) as the base case. More directly, we have by
[
9
, Theorem 7.4.2]
that
\bigoplus_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert=d}\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}(i^{(\mathbf{x})},i^{(\mathbf{y})})
is isomorphic to the classical Schur algebra
S_{\mathbbm{k}}(d,d)
, and from this point of view, (
3.4.2
) merely expresses Green’s product rule (see
[
14
, (2.3b)]
) applied to the product

\xi_{1^{y_{1}}2^{y_{2}}\cdots n^{y_{n}},1^{d}}\cdot\xi_{1^{d},1^{x_{1}}2^{x_{2}}\cdots m^{x_{m}}}
.
∎

We will say a finitely supported function
\mu:{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\rightarrow\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
is a
restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
-composition
provided that
\mu(b)\leq 1
whenever
\overline{b}=\bar{1}
. We define the following associated values:

\displaystyle|\mu|=\sum_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\mu(b),\qquad\{\mu\}^{!}=\prod_{b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}}\mu(b)!,\qquad\{\mu\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\\
b\in\mathfrak{a}\end{subarray}}\mu(b)!,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{\mu^{\vee}\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\\
b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a}\end{subarray}}\mu(b)!.

Then for such
\mu
, we enumerate
\textup{supp}(\mu)=\{b^{(1)}_{\mu}>\cdots>b^{(d_{\mu})}_{\mu}\}
, where
d_{\mu}=|\textup{supp}(\mu)|
, and define the following morphisms:

For
t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we write
{}_{j}\mathcal{B}^{t}_{i}
for the set of restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
-compositions
\mu
such that
|\mu|=t
. Then we set
{}_{j}\mathcal{B}_{i}=\bigcup_{t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}}{}_{j}\mathcal{B}_{i}^{t}
. For any
m\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
i,j,k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\in I
,
x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}

The assumption that
\mathcal{A}
is a Frobenius great pair implies that either
b\in\mathfrak{a}
or
b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a}
for each
b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
. This, in turn, implies
\{\mu\}^{!}
evenly divides the product
\{\mu\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}\{\mu^{\vee}\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}
and, hence, the coefficients in the above sums are integers that can be viewed as elements of
\mathbbm{k}
.
We call elements of the form
Eq.

4.0.4
(
x
-thick
)
teleporters
, as they can ‘teleport’ coupons from one corner of the barbell shape to the other, see
Lemma

4.1.3
. These may be viewed as thickened versions of the teleporters in
[
7
]
.

4.1.
Teleporter relations

Although the definition of the thick teleporter decorations above is somewhat dense and combinatorial, we show below that, morally speaking, the
x
-thick teleporter is obtained by aggregating
x
many thin teleporters.

Lemma 4.1.1
.

For all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
i,j\in I
, in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
we have:

Proof.

We prove the first statement, the second being similar. We argue by induction on
x
, with the base case
x=1
trivial. Assuming the claim holds for
x
, we have:

\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(x+1)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+1)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle\ddots
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+1)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(x+1)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(1)}
\scriptstyle\ddots

(4.1.1)

\xi(\mu,b)=\begin{cases}(\mu(b)+1)^{2}&\textup{if }b\in\mathfrak{a},\;b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a};\\
\mu(b)+1&\textup{if }b\in\mathfrak{a},\;b^{\vee}\notin\mathfrak{a}\textup{ or }b\in\mathfrak{a},\;b^{\vee}\in\mathfrak{a};\\
1&\textup{if }b\in A_{\bar{1}},\mu(b)=0;\\
0&\textup{if }b\in A_{\bar{1}},\mu(b)=1.\end{cases}

Now, for
b\in\textup{supp}(\mu)
, we write
\mu\backslash b
for the restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}
-composition given by setting
(\mu\backslash b)(c)=\mu(c)-\delta_{c,b}
. Then after reindexing we write the above sum:

Finally, note that by consideration of
Eq.

4.1.1
, we have

\frac{\{\mu\backslash b\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}\{(\mu\backslash b)^{\vee}\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}}{\{(\mu\backslash b)\}^{!}}\xi(\mu\backslash b,b)=\frac{\{\mu\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}\{\mu^{\vee}\}^{!}_{\mathfrak{a}}}{\{\mu\}^{!}}\mu(b)

for all
\mu\in{}_{j}\mathcal{B}_{i}^{x+1}
and
b\in\textup{supp}(\mu)
. Moreover
\sum_{b\in\textup{supp}(\mu)}\mu(b)=x+1
for all
\mu\in{}_{j}\mathcal{B}_{i}^{x+1}
. Thus it follows that
Eq.

4.1.2
is equal to

Finally, we show that the thick teleporter decorations are worthy of the name; they ‘teleport’ a thick coupon from one corner of the teleporter to the other.

Lemma 4.1.3
.

For all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
i,j\in I
,
f\in{}_{i}A^{(x)}_{k}
,
g\in{}_{j}A^{(x)}_{\ell}
,

\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 37.35571pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-37.35571pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-43.12904pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to74.71pt{\vbox to86.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 36.91357pt\lower-15.1338pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}

Proof.

When
x=1
, the claims follow from
Lemma

2.4.3
. For
x>1
, we note that if we multiply both sides of the equalities above by
x!
, then this equality follows from the
x=1
case together with

4.1.1
and
3.2.11
. But morphism spaces in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
are
\mathbbm{k}
-free by

, Corollary 6.6.3]
, which implies the result.
∎

5.
The affine Frobenius web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

5.1.
The category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

Let
\mathcal{A}=((A,a)_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a Frobenius great pair. The affine web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
is defined by adding additional “polynomial” generating morphisms to the finite web category
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
that are drawn as a black dot.

Definition 5.1.1
.

Let
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
be the strict monoidal
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory defined as follows.
The objects and the monoidal structure on objects are the same as in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
, given by
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
.
The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given by the diagrams:

(5.1.1)

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}

\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(z)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(z)}

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(z)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(z)}

for
i,j\in I
,
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
z\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
,
f\in jA^{(z)}i
.
The
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading is given by declaring that splits, merges, and crossings have parity
\bar{0}
, and the parity of the
f
coupon is
\bar{f}
. The new generators are called
affine dots
and are declared to be even. The relations between morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given as follows. The “non-dotted” relations (
3.2.2
)–(
3.2.12
) hold as in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
, together with the ‘dotted relations’ below.

:

5.2.
Affine degree

We will say an affine dot on a strand of thickness
z
has
affine degree

z
. More generally, we define the affine degree of a diagram representing a morphism in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
to be the sum of the affine degrees of the affine dot morphisms in the diagram. Note that relation
Eq.

5.1.3
means a given morphism in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
could be drawn using linear combinations of diagrams with differing affine degrees. For this reasons, when we use the notion of affine degree, it will be in reference to specific diagrams and linear combinations of diagrams.

5.3.
Some implied relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

There is an obvious
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal functor from
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
to
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
which takes objects and generating morphisms to their mates in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. This implies the relations established for
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
in
Sections

3.3
and
4
may be freely transferred to
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
, and we will use these implicitly.
We now highlight some additional implied relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

Lemma 5.3.1

As noted in
Section

2.4
, the element
\sum_{b\in{}_{j}B_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}
is independent of choice of basis for
{}_{j}A_{i}
. As
\{\psi^{-1}(c)\mid c\in{}_{j}B_{i}\}
is an alternate choice of basis for
jAi
, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{b\in{}_{j}B_{i}}b\otimes b^{\vee}=\sum_{c\in{}_{j}B_{i}}\psi^{-1}(c)\otimes(\psi^{-1}(c))^{\vee}=\sum_{c\in{}_{j}B_{i}}\psi^{-1}(c)\otimes\psi^{-1}(c^{\vee}).

6.2.
Restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}
-compositions

For
i,j\in I
, define the set:

\displaystyle{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}

\displaystyle:=\{(t,b)\mid t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0},b\in{}_{j}\mathtt{B}_{i}\},

and set
\mathtt{P}:=\bigsqcup_{i,j\in I}{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}
. Fix a total order
>
on
\mathtt{B}
. We extend the total order on
\mathtt{B}
to a total order on
\mathtt{P}
by setting
[t,b]>[t^{\prime},b^{\prime}]
whenever
t>t^{\prime}
or
t=t^{\prime}
and
b>b^{\prime}
.
We say a finitely supported function
\mu:{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}\rightarrow\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
is a
restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}
-composition
provided that
\mu(t,b)\leq 1
whenever
\bar{b}=\bar{1}
. We write
|\mu|=\sum_{(t,b)\in{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}}\mu(t,b)\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
. For such
\mu
, we enumerate

\displaystyle\textup{supp}(\mu)=\{(t_{\mu}^{(1)},b_{\mu}^{(1)})>(t_{\mu}^{(2)},b_{\mu}^{(2)})>\cdots>(t_{\mu}^{(d_{\mu})},b_{\mu}^{(d_{\mu})})\},

where
d_{\mu}=|\textup{supp}(\mu)|
. We write
{}_{j}\mathcal{P}_{i}
for the set of restricted
{}_{j}\mathtt{P}_{i}
-compositions. We will freely associate
{}_{j}\mathcal{B}_{i}
with the subset

\displaystyle\{\mu\in{}_{j}\mathcal{P}_{i}\mid\mu(t,b)=0\textup{ for all }t>0\}\subseteq{}_{j}\mathcal{P}_{i}.

We now generalize the notation of
Eq.

4.0.3
to any
\mu\in{}_{j}\mathcal{P}_{i}
, by defining the associated morphisms in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}(i^{(|\mu|)},j^{(|\mu|)})
:

(6.2.1)

\displaystyle{}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 13.37096pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-13.37096pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-36.30046pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to26.74pt{\vbox to72.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 13.37096pt\lower-15.1338pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 28.35}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}

6.3.
(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
-matrices

We say
\bm{\mu}=(\mu_{r,s})_{r\in[1,|\mathbf{x}|],s\in[1,|\mathbf{y}|]}
is an
(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
-matrix
provided

(1)

\mu_{r,s}\in{}_{j_{s}}\mathcal{P}_{i_{r}}
for
r\in[1,|\mathbf{x}|]
,
s\in[1,|\mathbf{y}|]
;

(2)

\sum_{t=1}^{|x|}|\mu_{t,s}|=y_{s}
for
s\in[1,|\mathbf{y}|]
;

(3)

\sum_{u=1}^{|y|}|\mu_{r,u}|=x_{r}
for
r\in[1,|\mathbf{x}|]
.

We write
\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
for the set of all
(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
-matrices. For
\bm{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
we define the associated morphism which we call a ‘decorated double coset diagram’:

\displaystyle\eta_{\bm{\mu}}=\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{{}}}}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 339.26802pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-339.26802pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-2.50174pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\begin{overpic}[WebAffImages/aff_base_diag.pdf]

Intuitively, this diagram can be thought of as follows. Let
k\in[1,r]
,
\ell\in[1,s]
,
t\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
b\in{}_{j_{\ell}}\mathtt{B}_{\psi^{-t}(i_{k})}
, and assume
\mu_{k,\ell}(t,b)=m
. If
b\in\mathfrak{a}
, then
\eta_{\bm{\mu}}
has a strand of thickness
m
which emanates from the
k
th component at the bottom of the diagram, and carries
t
affine dots and the coupon
b
into the
\ell
th component at the top of the diagram. On the other hand, if
b\notin\mathfrak{a}
, then
\eta_{\bm{\mu}}
has
m
many thin strands which emanate from the
k
th component at the bottom of the diagram, each carrying
t
affine dots and the coupon
b
to the
\ell
th component at the top of the diagram. See
Example

6.3.1
for an exemplar of the morphism
\eta_{\bm{\mu}}
.

Given
d\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we set

\displaystyle\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})_{\leq d}:=\mathbbm{k}\{\eta_{\bm{\mu}}\mid\bm{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})}),\eta_{\bm{\mu}}\textup{ has affine degree}\leq d\}

Recall that
we write
i^{x}:=(i^{(1)})^{x}
, and
if
\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})}=i_{1}^{(x_{1})}\cdots i_{r}^{(x_{r})}
, then we write
\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}}=i_{1}^{x_{1}}\cdots i_{r}^{x_{r}}
.
Let
\bm{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
.
Recalling
Eq.

6.2.2
, we define
\hat{\bm{\mu}}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{j}^{\mathbf{x}})
to be the ‘cabling’ of
\bm{\mu}
, so that

\displaystyle\eta_{\hat{\bm{\mu}}}=\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{{}}}}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 603.78615pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-603.78615pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\begin{overpic}[WebAffImages/aff_base_cabled.pdf]
\put(15.0,-5.0){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{$\scriptstyle\underbrace{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx\color[rgb]{0,0,0}}}_{x_{1}\textup{times}}$}}
\put(48.0,-5.0){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{$\scriptstyle\underbrace{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx\color[rgb]{0,0,0}}}_{x_{2}\textup{times}}$}}
\put(85.0,-5.0){\pic@makebox@{\makebox}{}(0.0,0.0)[t]{$\scriptstyle\underbrace{\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx\color[rgb]{0,0,0}}}_{x_{m}\textup{times}}$}}

6.4.
A spanning set for
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

Lemma 6.4.1
.

Let
D\in\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
be a diagram of affine degree
d
. Then
D\in\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})_{\leq d}
.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on
d
. When
d=0
, this result follows as in the proof of
[
9
, Proposition 6.5.1]
. For
d>0
, note that thanks to
Eq.

5.1.3
, crossings intertwine affine dots modulo
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combinations of diagrams of lower affine degree. Hence by the induction assumption we may similarly follow the proof of
[
9
, Proposition 6.5.1]
, treating affine dots as coupons in that setting, arriving at the result. ∎

Corollary 6.4.2
.

The diagrams
\{\eta_{\bm{\mu}}\mid\bm{\mu}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})\}
form a
\mathbbm{k}
-spanning set for
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{i}^{(\mathbf{x})},\mathbf{j}^{(\mathbf{y})})
.

7.
The thin dot web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}

7.1.
The category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}

We next introduce the following simplified version of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
where the only allowed affine dot generators are those on strands of thickness one. The defining relations are exactly those of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
applied to this restricted set of generators. It will be helpful in certain upcoming arguments and can be viewed as an alternate presentation of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
when
\mathbbm{k}
is a field (see
Corollary

7.3.2
).

Definition 7.1.1
.

Let
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
be the strict monoidal
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory defined as follows.
The objects and the monoidal structure on objects are the same as in
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
, given by
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}})=\widehat{\Omega}_{I}
.
The generating morphisms of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
are given by the diagrams:

It is immediate from the definition that there is a monoidal superfunctor

(7.1.3)

\iota=\iota_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

which is the identity on objects and sends every web diagram in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
to its mate in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

7.2.
Implied relations in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
Over a Field

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be a characteristic zero field that contains
\mathbbm{k}
. Throughout this section we work over
\mathbbm{K}
. Let
\mathcal{A}=\left((A,\mathfrak{a})_{I},\mathrm{tr},\psi\right)
be a Frobenius great pair defined over
\mathbbm{K}
. For example,
\mathcal{A}
could have been obtained from a Frobenius great pair defined over
\mathbbm{k}
by extending scalars to
\mathbbm{K}
. While in general there are no thick affine dots in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
, replacement morphisms can be defined over
\mathbbm{K}
for
i\in I
and
x\geq 1
by

Proof.

If
x=0
or
y=0
, the claim is trivial. We first prove the claim holds for
y=1
and all
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{>0}
, by induction on
x
. The base case
x=1
follows from the defining relations. Now fix
x>1
and assume that
Eq.

7.2.2
holds for
y=1
and
x-1
. Then we have:

7.3.
Equivalence of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
and
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
Over a Field

If
\mathbbm{K}
is a field which contains
\mathbbm{k}
and
\mathcal{A}
is a Frobenius great pair defined over
\mathbbm{k}
, then let
\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}
denote the Frobenius great pair obtained from
\mathcal{A}
by extending scalars to
\mathbbm{K}
.
