Proof.

Since
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}}
is defined as a
\mathbbm{K}
-linear monoidal category, the white dots are sensible morphisms in this category and, hence, the given assignment of generating morphisms is allowed. The claim is proven by verifying that the defining relations of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
are satisfied. This is immediate from the relations proven in this section.
∎

Corollary 7.3.2
.

When
\mathbbm{k}
is a field of characteristic zero and
\mathcal{A}
is a Frobenius great pair defined over
\mathbbm{k}
, then the functor from
Eq.

7.1.3
,

\iota_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}},

is an isomorphism of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear monoidal categories

Proof.

An easy application of
Eqs.

5.1.2
and
3.2.4
shows that
\iota_{\mathcal{A}}
and the functor
\kappa_{\mathcal{A}}
from
Theorem

7.3.1
are mutual inverses.
∎

Remark 7.3.3
.

The functor
\iota_{\mathcal{A}}
will always be essentially surjective and faithful. Essential surjectivity is obvious and faithfulness is an immediate consequence of Corollary
6.4.2
.

8.
The defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}

In this section we recall some of the main results from
[
9
]
about the defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
on the supercategory of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules. We upgrade this to a defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
in
Section

9
.

8.1.
The supercategory of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules

For
n\geq 1
, let
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
be the free
\mathbbm{k}
-module of
n\times n
matrices with entries in
A
. For
r,s\in[1,n]
and
f\in A
, write
E_{r,s}^{f}
for the
n\times n
matrix with
(r,s)
-entry equal to
f
and all other entries equal to zero. The
\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
-grading on
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
is given by declaring
\overline{E_{r,s}^{f}}=\overline{f}
for all homogeneous
f\in A
. The set of matrices
\{E_{r,s}^{b}\mid r,s\in[1,n]\text{ and }b\in\mathtt{B}\}
form a homogeneous
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
.

We view
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
as a Lie superalgebra over
\mathbbm{k}
via the graded commutator bracket,

\displaystyle[E_{r,s}^{f},E_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime}}^{f^{\prime}}]=\delta_{s,r^{\prime}}E_{r,s^{\prime}}^{ff^{\prime}}-(-1)^{\bar{f}\bar{f}^{\prime}}\delta_{s^{\prime},r}E_{r^{\prime},s}^{f^{\prime}f},

for all
r,s,r^{\prime},s^{\prime}\in[1,n]
and homogeneous
f,f^{\prime}\in A
. Write
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
for the universal enveloping superalgebra of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
.

We will be interested in the category of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules,
\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. Our convention is to write
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphisms on the left and to allow for all (not just parity preserving) homomorphisms. That is, a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
f:M\rightarrow N
between right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules is a homomorphism if
f(mu)=f(m)u
for all
m\in M
and
u\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. The space of supermodule homomorphisms
{\rm Hom}_{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)}(M,N)
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule where the grading is given by declaring the parity of
f
to be
s\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
if
f(M_{r})\subset N_{r+s}
for
r\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
.

The coproduct on
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is given by
\Delta(u)=1\otimes u+u\otimes 1
for
u\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. Explicitly, if
M
and
N
are
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules, then
M\otimes N
is a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule via:

\displaystyle(m\otimes n)\cdot u=(-1)^{\overline{u}\,\overline{n}}mu\otimes n+m\otimes nu

for homogenous
m\in M
,
n\in N
, and
u\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. The trivial
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule is
\mathbbm{k}
(concentrated in degree
\bar{0}
) with
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
acting as zero. This data makes
\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
into a monoidal supercategory. The twist map given below makes it a symmetric monoidal supercategory.

8.2.
Symmetric powers

For
n\geq 1
, let
V=V_{n}:=A^{\oplus n}
denote the set of length
n
row vectors with entries in
A
. For
t\in[1,n]
and
a\in A
, we write
v_{t}^{a}\in V
for the row vector which has
a
in position
t
and is zero elsewhere. The set
\{v_{t}^{b}\mid t\in[1,n],b\in\mathtt{B}\}
is a homogeneous
\mathbbm{k}
-basis for
V
. Observe that
V_{n}
is naturally a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule with action given by right multiplication:

v_{t}^{a}\cdot E_{r,s}^{f}=\delta_{r,t}v_{s}^{af},

for
r,s,t\in[1,n]
and
a,f\in A
.
For each
i\in I
there is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-submodule
{}_{i}V={}_{i}V_{n}=(iA)^{\oplus n}\subseteq V_{n}
with homogeneous basis
\{v_{r}^{b}\mid r\in[1,n],b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}\}
.

Via the coproduct, the tensor powers
({}_{i}V)^{\otimes x}
for
x\geq 0
are
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules, as is the tensor algebra
T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)=\bigoplus_{x\geq 0}({}_{i}V)^{\otimes x}
. By convention,
({}_{i}V)^{\otimes 0}=\mathbbm{k}
for all
i\in I
.

Let
J
denote the two-sided ideal in
T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
generated by

\left\{v\otimes w-(-1)^{\bar{v}\bar{w}}w\otimes v\mid\text{ homogeneous }v,w\in{}_{i}V\right\}\cup\left\{v\otimes v\mid v\in\left({}_{i}V\right)_{\bar{1}}\right\}.

Let
S^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
denote the symmetric superalgebra
T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)/J
and let
p:T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)\rightarrow S^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
be the canonical map. Since
J
is a homogeneous ideal in the
\mathbbm{Z}
-grading on
T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
, we have
S^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)=\oplus_{x\geq 0}S^{x}_{i}V
, where
S^{x}_{i}V=S^{x}({}_{i}V)
is the image of
({}_{i}V)^{\otimes x}
under
p
. If we write
v_{i_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{x}}^{\alpha_{x}}
for
p(v_{i_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i_{x}}^{\alpha_{x}})
, then for each
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
i\in I
,
S^{x}_{i}V
has a
\mathbbm{k}
-basis given by the set

\left\{(v_{1}^{b_{1}})^{r_{1}}\dotsb(v_{n}^{b_{n}})^{r_{n}}\left|\;b_{1},\dotsc,b_{n}\in\mathtt{B},r_{k}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0},\sum_{k=1}^{n}r_{k}=x,\text{ and }r_{k}\in\{0,1\}\text{ whenever }\overline{b}_{k}=\bar{1}\right.\right\}.

Note that for all
i\in I
,
S^{0}_{i}V\cong\mathbbm{k}
and
S^{1}_{i}V\cong{}_{i}V
.

Since
J
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-submodule of
T^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
, the symmetric superalgebra
S^{\bullet}({}_{i}V)
and the symmetric powers
S^{x}_{i}V
are also
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules with the action given on homogeneous elements by

\displaystyle v_{r_{1}}^{f_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{f_{x}}\cdot E_{s,t}^{g}=\sum_{u=1}^{x}(-1)^{\bar{g}(\bar{f}_{u+1}+\cdots+\bar{f}_{x})}\delta_{r_{u}s}v_{r_{1}}^{f_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{u-1}}^{f_{u-1}}v_{t}^{f_{u}g}v_{u+1}^{f_{u+1}}\cdots v_{x}^{f_{x}}.

8.3.
Distinguished morphisms

Having defined the symmetric powers
S_{i}^{x}V
for
i\in I
and
x\geq 0
, we next define certain homomorphisms between tensor products of these
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules. These are discussed in greater detail in
[
9
, Section 5]
.

8.3.1.
The twist map

For any two
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules
M
and
N
, there is an even “twist” supermodule homomorphism:

\tau_{M,N}:M\otimes N\rightarrow N\otimes M,\qquad m\otimes n\mapsto(-1)^{\bar{m}\bar{n}}n\otimes m.

In particular, taking
i,j\in I
and
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, we have the special case of
M=S_{i}^{x}V
and
N=S_{j}^{y}V
and the associated
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism

\tau_{i^{x},j^{y}}:=\tau_{S_{i}^{x}V,S_{j}^{y}V}:S_{i}^{x}V\otimes S_{j}^{y}V\rightarrow S_{j}^{y}V\otimes S_{i}^{x}V.

8.3.2.
The split map

For any
i\in I
, we have the
split map

\textup{spl}_{i^{x},i^{y}}:S^{x+y}_{i}V\rightarrow S^{x}_{i}V\otimes S^{y}_{i}V
given by

(8.3.1)

\displaystyle\textup{spl}_{i^{x},i^{y}}(w_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{x+y})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}T=\{t_{1}<\cdots<t_{x}\}\\
U=\{u_{1}<\cdots<u_{y}\}\\
T\cup U=\{1,\ldots,x+y\}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\varepsilon(T,U)}w_{t_{1}}\cdots w_{t_{x}}\otimes w_{u_{1}}\cdots w_{u_{y}},

for all homogeneous
w_{1},\ldots,w_{x+y}\in{}_{i}V
, where
\varepsilon(T,U)\in\mathbbm{Z}_{2}
is defined by

\displaystyle\varepsilon(T,U)=\#\{(t,u)\in T\times U\mid t>u,\,\overline{w}_{t}=\overline{w}_{u}=\bar{1}\}.

The split map is an even supermodule homomorphism.

8.3.3.
The merge map

Similarly, for
i\in I
and
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, define the
merge map

\textup{mer}_{i^{x},i^{y}}:S^{x}_{i}V\otimes S^{x}_{i}V\rightarrow S^{x+y}_{i}V

by

(8.3.2)

\displaystyle\textup{mer}_{i^{x},i^{y}}(w_{1}\cdots w_{x}\otimes w_{1}^{\prime}\cdots w_{y}^{\prime})=w_{1}\cdots w_{x}w_{1}^{\prime}\cdots w_{y}^{\prime},

for all
w_{1},\ldots,w_{x},w_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,w_{y}^{\prime}\in{}_{i}V
. Again, this is an even supermodule homomomorphism.

8.3.4.
The left multiplication map

Fix
i,j\in I
and
x\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
, and suppose that
f\in jA^{(x)}i
. Left multiplication by
f
defines a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
{}_{i}A\rightarrow{}_{j}A
. With this in mind, there is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism with parity
\bar{f}
,

L_{x}^{f}:S^{x}_{i}V\rightarrow S^{x}_{j}V,

given by

(8.3.3)

\displaystyle L_{x}^{f}(v_{r_{1}}^{g_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{g_{x}})=v_{r_{1}}^{fg_{1}}\cdots v_{r_{x}}^{fg_{x}}

for all
r_{k}\in[1,n]
and homogenous
g_{k}\in{}_{i}V
. Note that when
x\geq 2
,
\bar{f}=\bar{0}
, so there is no need to worry about signs.

8.4.
The defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}

The following theorem is
[
9
, Theorem 5.5.1]
. We call this functor the defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

n\geq 1
. Then there is a monoidal superfunctor

\displaystyle G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)

.

8.5.
The category
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))

Let
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
denote the monoidal supercategory of endofunctors of
\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. That is, the objects are functors
F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
and the morphisms are natural transformations between functors. Our convention is that the monoidal product
\odot
in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
is the left-to-right composition of functors. That is, if
F,G:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
are objects in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
, then their monoidal product
F\odot G
is the endofunctor given by first applying
F
and then applying
G
. We refer to
[
4
, Example 1.5]
for details on these notions in the graded setting, noting their convention is for the monoidal product to be given by the right-to-left composition of functors.

For each
n\geq 1
there is a monoidal functor
\Phi:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
defined by “tensoring on the right” as follows. For a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermoduile
N
,
\Phi(N)=\Phi_{N}
is the functor
-\otimes N:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
On morphisms, a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module homomorphism
f:N\rightarrow N^{\prime}
goes to the natural transformation given by
\Phi(f)_{M}:={\rm Id}_{M}\otimes f:M\otimes N\rightarrow M\otimes N^{\prime}
for every right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module
M
. Wanting
\Phi
to be monoidal explains our convention for composing endofuctors left-to-right; namely, given our choices, we have

(-\otimes M)\odot(-\otimes N)=-\otimes\left(M\otimes N\right).

Composing the monoidal functor
\Phi
with the functor
G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
from
Theorem

8.4.1
yields the following result.

Lemma 8.5.1
.

For every
n\geq 1
there is a monoidal superfunctor

\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{n}:=\Phi\circ G_{n}:\mathbf{Web}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))

given on generating objects by
\widehat{G}_{n}\left(i^{(x)}\right)=-\otimes S^{x}_{i}V_{n}
, and on generating morphisms by

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\displaystyle\mapsto-\otimes\textup{spl}_{i^{x},i^{y}}

\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(y)}

\displaystyle\mapsto-\otimes\tau_{i^{x},j^{y}},

\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(y)}
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x+y)}

\displaystyle\mapsto-\otimes\textup{mer}_{i^{x},i^{y}},

\scriptstyle f
\scriptstyle i^{\scriptstyle(x)}
\scriptstyle j^{\scriptstyle(x)}

\displaystyle\mapsto-\otimes L_{x}^{f},

for all
x,y\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
,
i,j\in I
, and
f\in jA^{(x)}i
.

9.
Casimir natural transformations and the defining representation of
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}

The goal of this section is to construct a representation of the affine web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
defined over the integral domain
\mathbbm{k}
to the supercategory of endofunctors for the general linear Lie superalgebra.

9.1.
The thin Casimir natural transformation

Fix
n\geq 1
. For
i\in I
,
\Phi({}_{i}V)=-\otimes{}_{i}V
defines an endofunctor of
\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. The goal of this section is to define an (even) natural transformation
C^{i}:-\otimes{}_{i}V\rightarrow-\otimes{}_{i}V_{n}
for every
i\in I
using the Casimir elements from
Section

2.4
.

Let
M
be a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module. Define a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
C_{M}:M\otimes V\rightarrow M\otimes V
by

(9.1.1)

C_{M}(m\otimes v^{\alpha}_{t})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

for homogeneous
m\in M
and
\alpha\in A
, and
t\in[1,n]
. While
\mathtt{B}
and the sum are potentially infinite, local finiteness ensures all but finitely many terms in the sum are zero.

Remark 9.1.1
.

In contemplating the above formula, readers may find it helpful to note that, after applying a teleporter-like result as discussed in
Remark

9.1.2
below, the linear map
C_{M}
factors as the composition

C_{M}=(1\otimes\psi^{-1})\circ\Omega:M\otimes V\rightarrow M\otimes V,

where:

•

the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
\psi^{-1}:V\rightarrow V
is given by applying the inverse Nakayama automorphism to the entries of the row vectors. That is,
\psi^{-1}(v_{r}^{\alpha})=v_{r}^{\psi^{-1}(\alpha)}
, and

•

the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
\Omega:M\otimes V\rightarrow M\otimes V
is defined as right multiplication by the element

\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B},r,s\in[1,n]}E_{r,s}^{b}\otimes E_{s,r}^{\psi(b)^{\vee}},

where
\psi(b)^{\vee}\in A
is the dual to
\psi(b)
with respect to the basis
\psi(\mathtt{B})=\{\psi(c)\mid c\in\mathtt{B}\}
.

In particular, when
\psi
is the identity map, the linear map
C_{M}
is equal to right multiplication by
\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B},r,s\in[1,n]}E_{r,s}^{b}\otimes E_{s,r}^{{b}^{\vee}}
.

Remark 9.1.2
.

In what follows, we will freely (and without further remark) apply teleporter results like Lemma
2.4.3
more widely and involving other algebraic objects, whenever their use is justified via a map from
A\otimes A
into the object. For instance, if
M,N
are
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules, with
f\in{}_{j}A_{i}
, then we have

\displaystyle\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{k}}(-1)^{\bar{b}\bar{n}+\bar{f}\bar{n}}mE_{r,s}^{fb}\otimes nE_{t,u}^{b^{\vee}}=\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{k}}(-1)^{\bar{b}\bar{n}}mE_{r,s}^{b}\otimes nE_{t,u}^{b^{\vee}f},

and

\displaystyle\sum_{b\in{}_{k}\mathtt{B}_{j}}(-1)^{\bar{b}\bar{n}+\bar{f}\bar{n}}mE_{r,s}^{bf}\otimes nE_{t,u}^{b^{\vee}}=\sum_{b\in{}_{k}\mathtt{B}_{j}}(-1)^{\bar{b}\bar{n}}mE_{r,s}^{b}\otimes nE_{t,u}^{\psi^{-1}(f)b^{\vee}}.

Indeed, note that there is a linear map

\displaystyle h:A\otimes A\rightarrow M\otimes N,\qquad g\otimes h\mapsto(-1)^{\bar{g}\bar{n}}mE_{r,s}^{g}\otimes nE_{t,u}^{h}.

By
Lemma

2.4.3
it follows that

\displaystyle h\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{k}}fb\otimes b^{\vee}\right)=h\left(\sum_{b\in{}_{i}\mathtt{B}_{k}}b\otimes b^{\vee}f\right),

for all
k\in I
, which yields the claimed result.

Lemma 9.1.3
.

For all
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules
M
the map
C_{M}
is a homomorphism of right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules.

Proof.

Given homogeneous
m\in M
,
\alpha,f\in A
, and
u,w\in[1,n]
, one has

\displaystyle C_{M}((m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})\cdot E^{f}_{u,w})

\displaystyle=C_{M}((-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}}mE_{u,w}^{f}\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha}+\delta_{t,u}m\otimes v^{\alpha f}_{w})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE^{f}_{u,w}E^{b\alpha}_{r,t}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}\delta_{t,u}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{f}\bar{b}}mE^{b\alpha f}_{r,w}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}.

On the other hand,

\displaystyle C_{M}(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})\cdot E_{u,w}^{f}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}\right)\cdot E_{u,w}^{f}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{b}\bar{f}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}E_{u,w}^{f}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}\delta_{r,u}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{u,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}f}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE^{f}_{u,w}E^{b\alpha}_{r,t}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}\delta_{t,u}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{f}\bar{b}}mE^{b\alpha f}_{r,w}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle\hskip 14.22636pt+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}\delta_{r,w}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+\color[rgb]{0,0,0}1}mE_{u,t}^{fb\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}\delta_{r,u}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{u,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}f}

where the last equality follows from the commutator formula for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. From the above displayed equation, we see that
C_{M}(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})\cdot E_{u,w}^{f}
is the sum of four expressions. The first two expressions precisely match the calculation of
C_{M}(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha}\cdot E_{u,w}^{f})
and, hence, the difference
C_{M}(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})\cdot E_{u,w}^{f}-C_{M}((m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})\cdot E^{f}_{u,w})
equals the sum of the last two expressions. By removing terms where the Kronecker delta function evaluates to zero this difference reduces to

(9.1.2)

\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+1}mE_{u,t}^{fb\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{u,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}f}.

By a teleporter argument along the lines of
Remark

9.1.2
, we have

\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+1}mE_{u,t}^{fb\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}}=\sum_{b\in\mathtt{B}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+1}mE_{u,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{w}^{b^{\vee}f}.

Therefore,
Eq.

9.1.2
equals zero and this implies the result.
∎

Lemma 9.1.4
.

Suppose
M
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule. For any homogeneous
f\in A
, let
L_{M}^{f}:M\otimes V\rightarrow M\otimes V
be the
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism given by:

L_{M}^{f}(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})=(-1)^{\bar{m}\bar{f}}m\otimes v_{t}^{f\alpha},

for
m\in M
,
1\leq t\leq n
, and
\alpha\in A
. Then,

C_{M}\circ L_{M}^{f}=L_{M}^{{}_{1}f}\circ C_{m}.

In particular, for every
i\in I
the restriction of
C_{M}
defines a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism

C_{M}^{i}:M\otimes{}_{i}V\rightarrow M\otimes{}_{i}V.

Proof.

For homogeneous
m\in M
,
v_{t}^{\alpha}\in V
, and
f\in A
, we have:

\displaystyle(L^{{}_{1}f}_{M}\circ C_{M})(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})

\displaystyle=L^{{}_{1}f}_{M}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}\right)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{f}\bar{m}+\bar{f}\,\bar{b}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{{{}_{1}f}b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}+\bar{f}\bar{m}+\bar{f}\,\bar{b}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}+\bar{\alpha}\bar{f}}mE_{r,t}^{bf\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{(\bar{\alpha}+\bar{f})\bar{b}+\bar{f}\bar{m}}mE_{r,t}^{bf\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=C_{M}((-1)^{\overline{f}\bar{m}}m\otimes v_{t}^{f\alpha})

\displaystyle=(C_{M}\circ L^{f}_{M})(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha}).

The second equality follows from an application of the transporter trick as described in
Remark

9.1.2
. This proves the main claim of the lemma.

For the next claim, fix
i\in I
. Since the Nakayama automorphism fixes the elements of
I
, the previous calculation shows that

C_{M}\circ L^{i}_{M}=L^{i}_{M}\circ C_{M}.

However, since
M\otimes{}_{i}V
is the image of
L^{i}_{M}
this equality implies the restriction of the supermodule homomorphism
C_{M}
defines an endomorphism of
M\otimes{}_{i}V
.
∎

Proposition 9.1.5
.

Fix
i\in I
. As
M
varies over all
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules, the collection of maps
C^{i}_{M}:M\otimes{}_{i}V\rightarrow M\otimes{}_{i}V
defines the data of a natural transformation

C^{i}:-\otimes{}_{i}V\rightarrow-\otimes{}_{i}V.

Proof.

Assume that
M,N
are right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules and that
\phi:M\rightarrow N
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism. We must verify that the following diagram commutes:

Given homogeneous
m\in M
and
v^{\alpha}_{t}\in{}_{i}V
,

\displaystyle\left(\phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{{}_{i}V}\circ C^{i}_{M}\right)(m\otimes v^{i\alpha}_{t})

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}\phi(mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha})\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}\phi(m)E_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=\left(C^{i}_{N}\circ\phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{{}_{i}V}\right)(m\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha}).

∎

9.2.
A representation of the thin dot category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}

The following lemma establishes a representation for the thin dot category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
into the endofunctor category
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
. The remainder of this section will be devoted to extending this representation to one of the full affine web category
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

on

. This verifies the relation, and the lemma follows.

9.3.
Extension of scalars and torsion

Let
\mathbbm{K}
be the field of fractions for
\mathbbm{k}
. For a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear supercategory
\bm{\mathcal{C}}
write
{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}
for the
\mathbb{K}
-linear category which has the same objects as
\bm{\mathcal{C}}
and whose morphisms are given by

{\rm Hom}_{{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(X,Y):=\mathbbm{K}\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}{\rm Hom}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(X,Y).

Composition of morphisms in
\bm{\mathcal{C}}
is extended linearly to define composition in
{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}
. It is straightforward to verify that
{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}
is a
\mathbb{K}
-linear supercategory.
There is a canonical functor

(9.3.1)

\xi=\xi_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}:\bm{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}

which is the identity on objects and
\alpha\mapsto{\rm Id}_{\mathbbm{K}}\otimes\alpha
on morphisms. If
\bm{\mathcal{D}}
is a
\mathbbm{K}
-linear category, then every functor of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear categories
\bm{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{D}}
extends uniquely to a functor of
\mathbbm{K}
-linear categories
{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{D}}
. Similarly, a functor of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear categories
F:\bm{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\bm{\mathcal{D}}
may be extended linearly to a
\mathbbm{K}
-linear functor
{}_{\mathbbm{K}}F:{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\bm{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\bm{\mathcal{D}}
.

Remark 9.3.1
.

Given a Frobenius great pair
\mathcal{A}
defined over
\mathbbm{k}
, write
\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}
for the Frobenius great pair defined over
\mathbbm{K}
by extending scalars. There are obvious functors between
{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
and
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}}
, and between
{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
and
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}}
. Each pair of functors define mutually inverse isomorphisms of monoidal
\mathbbm{K}
-linear categories. We identify these categories via these functors.

Recall that if
M
is a
\mathbbm{k}
-module, then
m\in M
is a
torsion element
if there is some non-zero
c\in\mathbbm{k}
with
cm=0
. The set of torsion elements of
M
is the
torsion submodule
of
M
, denoted by
T(M)
. One says that
M
is
torsion-free
if
T(M)=0
. For example, every free
\mathbbm{k}
-module is torsion-free.

Lemma 9.3.2
.

Suppose
M
and
F
are
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodules and assume
F
is torsion-free. Then, the
\mathbbm{k}
-supermodule of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear maps

{\rm Hom}_{\mathbbm{k}}(M,F)

is torsion-free.

The following lemma is immediate from
[
1
, Exercise 3.12.iv]
.

Lemma 9.3.3
.

For objects
X
and
Y
in a supercategory
\bm{\mathcal{C}}
, let

\xi_{X,Y}:{\rm Hom}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(X,Y)\rightarrow\mathbb{K}\otimes{\rm Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y).

denote the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map given by the canonical functor
\xi:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow{}_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{C}
.
Then the kernel of
\xi_{X,Y}
is the torsion submodule
T({\rm Hom}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(X,Y))
.

Lemma 9.3.4
.

Suppose
\Psi
and
\Phi
are functors in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
where
\Psi
is exact and
\Phi
preserves the subcategory of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules which are free over
\mathbbm{k}
. Then, the space of natural transformations
{\rm Hom}_{\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))}(\Psi,\Phi)
is torsion-free as a
\mathbbm{k}
-module.

Proof.

Suppose that
\eta:\Psi\rightarrow\Phi
is a non-zero natural transformation, and that
c\in\mathbbm{k}
is non-zero. We need to verify that the natural transformation
c\eta
is non-zero.

Because
\eta
is non-zero by assumption, there exists some
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule
M
for which the associated homomorphism
\eta_{M}:\Psi(M)\rightarrow\Phi(M)
is not the zero map. Fix a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule
F
which is free over
\mathbbm{k}
and admits an exact sequence:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0.}

That such an
F
exists follows by taking
F
to be a free cover of
M
as a right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodule. The PBW theorem guarantees that such an
F
is free over
\mathbbm{k}
.

Given the assumptions, there is the following commutative diagram with an exact top row:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi(F)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi(M)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(F)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi(M).}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{F}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{M}}

This diagram and the fact that
\eta_{M}
is non-zero immediately implies
\eta_{F}
is also non-zero.

The
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism
\eta_{F}
is
\mathbbm{k}
-linear and may be regarded as an element of
{\rm Hom}_{\mathbbm{k}}(\Psi(F),\Phi(F))
. However,
F
is a free
\mathbbm{k}
-module which implies
\Phi(F)
is also
\mathbbm{k}
-free and, hence, torsion-free. This, in turn, implies
{\rm Hom}_{\mathbbm{k}}(\Psi(F),\Phi(F))
is torsion-free by
Lemma

9.3.2
. Since
\eta_{F}
is non-zero, this implies
c\eta_{F}
is also nonzero and, hence, the natural transformation
c\eta
is nonzero.∎

9.4.
The thick Casimir

The goal of this section is to define a Casimir element for the thick affine dots.

Given a finite subset of positive integers,
S\subset\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 1}
, and
t\leq|S|
, we call an ordered sequence
\mathbf{u}=u_{1}\cdots u_{t}
a
t
-permutation of
S
(or simply
permutation of
S
if the
t
is left implicit) if
u_{1},\ldots,u_{t}
are distinct elements of
S
. We write
\ell(\mathbf{u}):=t
for the length of
\mathbf{u}
. We call a permutation
\mathbf{u}

least-last
provided that
u_{j}>u_{\ell(\mathbf{u})}
for
j\in[1,\ell(\mathbf{u})]
.
An
ordered
t
-partition of
S
is a sequence
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}=\mathbf{u}^{(1)}|\mathbf{u}^{(2)}|\cdots|\mathbf{u}^{(d)}
of permutations
\mathbf{u}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{u}^{(d)}
of
S
such that
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{(1)}\mathbf{u}^{(2)}\cdots\mathbf{u}^{(d)}
is a
t
-permutation of
S
. In other words, an ordered
t
-partition of
S
is a
t
-permutation of
S
equipped with a choice of grouping. We write
\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}):=d
for the number of permutations in
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}
. Write
\textup{ord}_{t}(S)
for the set of ordered
t
-partitions of
S
. For short we write
\textup{ord}_{k}
for
\textup{ord}_{k}([1,k])
for all
k\geq 1
.

For
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{t}(S)
, we say that
\mathbf{u}
is
good
provided that:

•

\mathbf{u}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{u}^{(\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))}
are least-last permutations, and;

•

u^{(1)}_{\ell(\mathbf{u}^{(1)})}<\cdots<u^{(\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))}_{\ell(\mathbf{u}^{(\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))})}
.

We write
\textup{ord}_{t}(S)^{\textup{g}}
for the set of good ordered
t
-partitions of
S
and write
\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}
for
\textup{ord}_{k}([1,k])^{\textup{g}}
. For a given
t
-permutation
\mathbf{u}
of
S
, there is a unique way to group the entries of
\mathbf{u}
to form a good ordered
t
-partition of
S
. Thus there is a bijection between
\textup{ord}_{t}(S)^{\textup{g}}
and
t
-permutations of
S
, and
|\textup{ord}_{t}(S)^{\textup{g}}|=|S|!/(|S|-t)!
.

Example 9.4.1
.

Let
S=\left\{1,2,3,5,6,7,11,13,29,74\right\}
. Then:

•

\mathbf{u}_{1}=6,29,74
,
\mathbf{u}_{2}=5,3,11,7,2,13
, and
\mathbf{u}_{3}=29,74,5,6,7,11,2,3,5
are permutations of
S
with
\ell(\mathbf{u}_{1})=3
,
\ell(\mathbf{u}_{2})=6
, and
\ell(\mathbf{u}_{3})=9
. None are least-last. However, both
29,74,6
and
74,29,6
are least-last
3
-partitions of
S
.

•

\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\bullet}=2,3|5,7,11|13
,
\mathbf{u}_{2}^{\bullet}=2|7,5|11,13,3
, and
\mathbf{u}_{3}^{\bullet}=2|11,13,3|7,5
are ordered
6
-partitions of
S
with
\ell(\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\bullet})=3
for
k=1,2,3
.
\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\bullet}
fails both conditions for being good,
\mathbf{u}_{2}^{\bullet}
satisfies the least-last condition but not the second condition, and
\mathbf{u}_{3}^{\bullet}
satisfies both.

For fixed
k,n\geq 1
, let
\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k})\in A^{k}
,
\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}),\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})\in[1,n]^{k}
. Let
\mathbf{w}=w_{1}\dotsb w_{t}
be a
t
-partition of
[1,k]
for some
t\leq k
. Using this data, set

\displaystyle E^{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{w})=\delta_{t_{w_{1}},r_{w_{2}}}\cdots\delta_{t_{w_{\ell(\mathbf{w})-1}},r_{w_{\ell(\mathbf{w})}}}E_{r_{w_{1}},t_{\ell(\mathbf{w})}}^{f_{w_{1}}\cdots f_{w_{\ell(\mathbf{w})}}}.

For
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}=\mathbf{u}^{(1)}|\cdots|\mathbf{u}^{(\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))}\in\textup{ord}_{k}
set
\mathbf{u}=u_{1}\ldots u_{k}
to be the
k
-partition of
[1,k]
obtained by removing the
|
symbols. With this data along with
\mathbf{f}
,
\mathbf{r}
, and
\mathbf{t}
from above, define:

\displaystyle E^{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}):=(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{u};\mathbf{f}\rangle}\prod_{x=1}^{\ell(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})}E^{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{(x)}),

where

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{u};\mathbf{f}\rangle:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<j\leq k\\
u_{i}>u_{j}\end{subarray}}\bar{f}_{u_{i}}\bar{f}_{u_{j}}.

For
\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}),\mathbf{g}=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{k})\in A^{k}
write
\mathbf{f}\mathbf{g}=(f_{1}g_{1},\ldots,f_{k}g_{k})\in A^{k}
, and set

\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{g},\mathbf{f}\rangle=\sum_{1\leq i\leq j\leq k}\bar{f}_{i}\bar{g}_{j}.

Definition 9.4.2
.

Let
M
be a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule. For
i\in I
and
k\geq 1
, define a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map

\displaystyle C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}=M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V\rightarrow M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V

by setting

\displaystyle m\otimes v_{t_{1}}^{f_{1}}\dotsb v_{t_{k}}^{f_{k}}\mapsto\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}.

for all homogeneous
m\in M
and
\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\dotsc,f_{k})\in(iA)^{k}
, and all
\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\dotsc,t_{k})\in[1,n]^{k}
.

Remark 9.4.3
.

Observe that
C_{M}^{i^{(1)}}
equals
C_{M}^{i}
.

Clearly the definition of the map
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
is rather complicated and would be difficult to use as given. The following result will allow us to avoid working with the definition of
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
directly. It can be interpreted as saying that
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
satisfies a special case of the rightmost relation in
Eq.

5.1.2
. See
Proposition

9.4.6
.

Proposition 9.4.4
.

Let
M
be a right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule. Then,

({\rm Id}_{M}\otimes\textup{mer}_{i^{k-1},i^{1}})\circ C_{M\otimes S_{i}^{k-1}V}^{i^{(1)}}\circ(C_{M}^{i^{(k-1)}}\otimes{\rm Id}_{S^{1}_{i}V})=C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}\circ({\rm Id}_{M}\otimes\textup{mer}_{i^{k-1},i^{1}})

as maps
M\otimes S_{i}^{k-1}V\otimes S_{i}^{1}V\rightarrow M\otimes S_{i}^{k}V
.

Proof.

First we define some combinatorial maps. For
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}
, and
w\in[1,k-1]
, let
\textup{bef}_{w}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}
be defined by inserting
k
directly before
w
in
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}
(in the same subpermutation as
w
). Let
\textup{suf}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})=\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}|k\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}
. It is straightforward to check that

(9.4.1)

\displaystyle\{\textup{bef}_{w}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\mid w\in[1,k-1],\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\}\sqcup\{\textup{suf}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\mid\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\}=\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}.

Now, let
m\in M
,
\mathbf{t}\in[1,n]^{k}
,
\mathbf{f}\in(iA)^{k}
. In what follows we will use primes to indicate the truncation of a
k
-tuple to the first
k-1
terms, writing
\mathbf{f}^{\prime}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k-1})
, and so forth. We have

\displaystyle\textup{mer}_{M}^{i^{(k-1)},\psi^{-1}(i)^{(1)}}\circ C_{M\otimes S_{i}^{k-1}V}^{i^{(1)}}\circ(C_{M}^{i^{(k-1)}}\otimes{\rm Id})(m\otimes v^{\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\otimes v_{t_{k}}^{f_{k}})

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\textup{mer}_{M}^{i^{(k-1)},\psi^{-1}(i)^{(1)}}\circ C_{M\otimes S_{i}^{k-1}V}^{i^{(1)}}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k-1}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k-1}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f}^{\prime},\mathbf{b}\rangle}mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k-1}}^{b_{k-1}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}\otimes v_{t_{k}}^{f_{k}}\right)

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\textup{mer}_{M}^{i^{(k-1)},\psi^{-1}(i)^{(1)}}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f}^{\prime},\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\rangle+\bar{b}_{k}\bar{f}_{k}}(mE^{\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k-1}}^{b_{k-1}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}})E_{r_{k},t_{k}}^{b_{k}f_{k}}\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\right)

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle+\bar{b}_{k}(\bar{b}_{1}+\cdots+\bar{b}_{k-1})}mE^{\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})E_{r_{k},t_{k}}^{b_{k}f_{k}}\otimes v_{r_{k-1}}^{b_{k-1}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}

\displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\\
w\in[1,k-1]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f}^{\prime},\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\rangle+(\bar{b}_{k}+\bar{f}_{k})(\bar{b}_{1}+\cdots+\bar{b}_{w-1})+\bar{b}_{k}\bar{f}_{k}}\delta_{r_{w},r_{k}}mE^{\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k-1}}^{b_{k-1}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{t_{k}}^{b_{w}^{\vee}b_{k}f_{k}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\textup{suf}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}

(9.4.2)

\displaystyle\hskip 42.67912pt+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k-1}^{\textup{g}}\\
w\in[1,k-1]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\textup{bef}_{w}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet}))\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}

(9.4.3)

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{v}^{\bullet}\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{v}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt=C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}\circ\;\textup{mer}_{M}^{i^{(k-1)},i^{(1)}}(m\otimes v^{\mathbf{f}^{\prime}}_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\otimes v_{t_{k}}^{f_{k}}),

where
Eq.

9.4.2
follows by an application of the transporter rule, and
Eq.

9.4.3
follows by
Eq.

9.4.1
, completing the proof.
∎

Theorem 9.4.5
.

The maps
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}:M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V\rightarrow M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V
define an even supernatural transformation,

C^{i^{(k)}}:-\otimes S^{k}_{i}V\rightarrow-\otimes S^{k}_{i}V,

in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
.

Proof.

Since
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
is only known to be
\mathbbm{k}
-linear, we must demonstrate that it is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism and that this family of maps satisfies the appropriate naturality condition. In fact, it turns out to be easier to first verify naturality.

Let
M,N
be two right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules and let
\varphi:M\rightarrow N
be a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism. Verifying the naturality condition amounts to demonstrating the commutativity of the following the square of
\mathbbm{k}
-linear maps:

(9.4.4)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\otimes S^{k}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes S^{k}_{i}(V)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces N\otimes S^{k}_{i}V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi\otimes{\rm Id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C_{N}^{i^{(k)}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi\otimes{\rm Id}}

For homogeneous
m\in M
and
\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\dotsc,f_{k})\in({}_{i}A)^{k}
, and
\mathbf{t}=(t_{1},\dotsc,t_{k})\in[1,n]^{k}
, write
m\otimes v_{\mathbf{t}}^{\mathbf{f}}=m\otimes v_{t_{1}}^{f_{1}}\dotsb v_{t_{k}}^{f_{k}}\in M\otimes S^{k}_{i}V
.
For such a vector, traveling along the top and then rightmost edge of the square results in:

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}\varphi(m)E^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}\in N\otimes S^{k}_{i}V.

Because
\varphi
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism and
E^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})
is the action of an element in
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
, we have:

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}\varphi(m)E^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{b}\in\mathtt{B}^{k}\\
\mathbf{r}\in[1,n]^{k}\\
\mathbf{u}\in\textup{ord}_{k}^{\textup{g}}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{b}\rangle}\varphi\left(mE^{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{u}^{\bullet})\right)\otimes v_{r_{k}}^{b_{k}^{\vee}}\cdots v_{r_{1}}^{b_{1}^{\vee}}.

However, the expression on the right side of the equality is also the result of instead traveling along the leftmost and bottom edges of the square. The commutativity of the square in
Eq.

9.4.4
follows.

Next, we establish that the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism for all
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodules
M
, all
i\in I
, and all
k\geq 1
. We prove this by induction on
k
. When
k=1
, the map
C_{M}^{i^{(1)}}
is the same as the thin Casimir
C^{i}_{M}
and the base case follows from
Lemma

9.1.4
. For the inductive step, given
K>1
suppose that
C_{M}^{i^{(k)}}
is a supermodule homomorphism for all
k<K
. We will show that
C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
is also a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism. First we establish that the scalar multiple
KC_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism. We have

9.4.4
. Using the induction hypothesis, the expression in the last line is a composite of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphisms. This proves
KC_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism for every right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module
M
.

We use this to show that
C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
itself is a supermodule homomorphism. For any fixed
X\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
define a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map

\eta_{M,X}:M\otimes S_{i}^{K}V\rightarrow M\otimes S_{i}^{K}V

by

\eta_{M,X}(w)=C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}(wX)-C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}(w)X,

where
w\in M\otimes S_{i}^{K}V
. Then
C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism if and only if
\eta_{M,X}
is identically zero for every
X\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
. Since
KC^{i^{(K)}}_{M}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-homomorphism for every
M
, it follows that
K\eta_{M,X}
is identically zero for all
X\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
and, hence,
\eta_{M,X}
is a torsion element in
\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(M\otimes S_{i}^{K}V\right)
.

Find a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule
F
which is free over
\mathbbm{k}
and admits an exact sequence

F\xrightarrow{\phi}M\rightarrow 0.

That such an
F
exists follows by taking a free cover of
M
as a right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-supermodule. The PBW theorem guarantees
F
is free over
\mathbbm{k}
.

Because
S_{i}^{K}V
is free over
\mathbbm{k}
, the functor
-\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}S_{i}^{K}(V)
is exact and the following diagram has exact rows:

(9.4.5)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\otimes S^{K}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes S^{K}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\otimes S^{K}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M\otimes S^{K}_{i}V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{S_{i}^{K}V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{F,X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{M,X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{S_{i}^{K}V}}

The fact that this diagram commutes follows from the definition of the map
\eta
, the naturality of
C^{i^{(K)}}
established above, and the fact that
\phi\otimes{\rm Id}_{S_{i}^{K}V}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism.

From the previous paragraph,
\eta_{F,X}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbbm{k}}\left(F\otimes S^{K}_{i}V\right)
is a torsion element. By
Lemma

9.3.2
this implies
\eta_{F,X}=0
. A diagram chase using
Eq.

9.4.5
implies
\eta_{M,X}=0
, as well. Since this is true for all
X\in\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
, we conclude that
C_{M}^{i^{(K)}}
is a
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-supermodule homomorphism.
∎

\mathbbm{K}

\mathbbm{k}
. Recall the functor
\kappa:\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathbbm{K}\otimes\mathcal{A}}\cong{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff},1}_{\mathcal{A}}
given by
Theorem

7.3.1
and the canonical functor
\xi:\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))\rightarrow{}_{\mathbb{K}}\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
discussed in
Section

9.3
. Starting with the representation
\widehat{H}_{n}
given in
Proposition

and extending scalars linearly yields the representation

The claim is that we can define the functor
H_{n}
as indicated and complete to a commuting square.
The definition of
H_{n}
on the generating objects and generating morphisms is clear given what each of the other three functors do to generating objects and morphisms, either by definition or by
Proposition

9.4.6
.

H_{n}
is well-defined, it remains to verify that the defining relations for
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
are satisfied. Given one of the defining relations, move terms to one side of the equality to obtain a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combination of diagrams,

, so that the condition

is equivalent to the relation being satisfied. For example, to the relation

, we associate the

For a general defining relation, we can express
R
as a
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combination of compositions of generating diagrams. We write
\tilde{R}
for the natural transformation in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
given by applying
H_{n}
to these generating diagrams, and then forming the corresponding
\mathbbm{k}
-linear combination of compositions of natural transformation in the obvious way (i.e., if
H_{n}
was a well-defined functor we would have
H_{n}(R)=\tilde{R}
). Checking that
H_{n}
is well-defined then amounts to checking that
\tilde{R}=0
as a natural transformation in
\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
.

Say that
R\in{\rm Hom}_{\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\left({\bf i}^{\bf x},{\bf j}^{\bf y}\right)
, where
{\bf i}^{\bf x}
and
{\bf j}^{\bf y}
are objects in
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. Since the above square commutes on generators, we have
\xi(\tilde{R})={}_{\mathbbm{K}}\widehat{H}_{n}(\kappa(R))=0
as a morphism in
{}_{\mathbbm{K}}\bm{\mathcal{End}}(\mathrm{mod}\text{-}\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
. Therefore, the morphism
\tilde{R}
is in the kernel of the
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map induced by
\xi
:

\displaystyle{\rm Hom}(-\otimes S_{\bf i}^{\bf x},-\otimes S^{\bf y}_{\bf j})\rightarrow\mathbb{K}\otimes{\rm Hom}(-\otimes S^{x_{1}}_{i_{1}}V\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{x_{t}}_{i_{t}}V,-\otimes S^{y_{1}}_{j_{1}}V\otimes\dotsb\otimes S^{y_{t^{\prime}}}_{j_{t^{\prime}}}V),

\displaystyle\eta\mapsto\xi(\eta)=1_{\mathbb{K}}\otimes\eta.

Because the functors in the domain and codomain of
H_{n}(R)
are exact and and take
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-modules which are free over
\mathbbm{k}
to others of the same kind,
Lemma

9.3.4
implies this
\mathbbm{k}
-linear map is injective and
\tilde{R}=0
, as desired.

∎

10.
The defining representation and the thin subcategory
\mathbf{Web}^{\textup{aff, thin}}_{\mathcal{A}}

Throughout this section we continue to let
\mathbbm{k}
be an integral domain. Our goal is to compute information about the action of
H_{n}(D)
for certain web diagrams
D
. This will be used to establish that the family of functors
\left\{H_{n}\right\}_{n\geq 1}
is asymptotically faithful on those diagrams.

10.1.
PBW bases and filtrations

Let
\mathcal{A}=(A,\mathrm{tr},\psi)
be a locally unital Frobenius superalgebra with set of distinguished idempotents
I
. Let
\mathtt{B}
be a homogeneous basis for
A
with a fixed total order.

Let
\mathfrak{h}\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
be the Lie subalgebra of diagonal matrices,
\mathfrak{b}\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
the subalgebra of upper triangular matricies,
\mathfrak{u}^{+}\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
the subalgebra of strictly upper triangular matrices, and
\mathfrak{u}^{-}\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
the subalgebra of strictly lower triangular matrices. There is a triangular decomposition
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)=\mathfrak{u}^{+}\oplus\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{u}^{-}
. Furthermore,
\mathfrak{u}^{+}
is an ideal of
\mathfrak{b}
and we have a canonical surjection

\mathfrak{b}\rightarrow\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{u}^{+}\cong\mathfrak{h}.

In particular, given a right
\mathfrak{h}
-supermodule we can and will view it as a right
\mathfrak{b}
-supermodule via inflation through this homomorphism.

For short, write
h_{k}^{a}=E_{k,k}^{a}
for
k=1,\dotsc,n
and
a\in A
. Then,

(10.1.1)

\left\{E_{i,j}^{b}\mid 1\leq i,j\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}\right\}

and

(10.1.2)

\left\{h_{k}^{b}\mid 1\leq k\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}\right\}

are homogeneous bases for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
and
\mathfrak{h}
, respectively. The total order on
\mathtt{B}
and the natural ordering on
[1,n]
can be used to define a total order on the bases for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
by declaring
E_{p_{1},q_{1}}^{b_{1}}\leq E_{p_{2},q_{2}}^{b_{2}}
if and only if
(p_{1},q_{1},b_{1})
is less than or equal to
(p_{2},q_{2},b_{2})
in the lexicographic ordering. With this ordering there is a corresponding PBW basis for
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
and
U(\mathfrak{h})
given by the set of all ordered monomials in the above bases for
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
and
\mathfrak{h}
, respectively.
Specifically, a PBW basis element of
U(\mathfrak{h})
is an ordered product

(10.1.3)

\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{i}\right)^{t_{i,b}},

where all but finitely many
t_{i,b}
are equal to zero, and
where
t_{i,b}\in\mathbbm{Z}_{\geq 0}
if
\bar{b}=\bar{0}
, and
t_{i,b}\in\{0,1\}
if
\bar{b}=\bar{1}
. We define the
degree
of this PBW basis element to be
\sum_{1\leq i\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}}t_{i,b}
. For a nonnegative integer
t
, set
U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq t}
to be the
\mathbbm{k}
-span of the PBW basis elements of degree less than or equal to
t
. The commutator formula,

(10.1.4)

h_{k}^{b}h_{r}^{a}=(-1)^{\bar{b}\bar{a}}h_{r}^{b}h_{k}^{a}+\delta_{k,r}h_{k}^{[b,a]},

shows that there is a multiplicative filtration

0\subseteq U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq 0}\subseteq U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq 1}\subseteq U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq 2}\subseteq(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq 3}\subseteq\dotsb.

For
t\geq 0
we write
U(\mathfrak{h})^{t}
for the
\mathbbm{k}
-span of the PBW basis elements of degree exactly
t
. Observe that the associated graded superalgebra
\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak{h})
is the free supercommutative
\mathbbm{k}
-superalgebra on generators
\left\{h_{k}^{b}\mid 1\leq k\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}\right\}
. In particular,
U(\mathfrak{h})^{t}
is isomorphic as a
\mathbbm{k}
-module in an obvious way to the degree
t
component of
\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak{h})
and we will identify them.

We define the
generic Verma module
,
\mathcal{M}
, to be the
(U(\mathfrak{h}),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bimodule

\mathcal{M}:=U(\mathfrak{h})\otimes_{U(\mathfrak{b})}U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)).

The PBW theorem applied to
\mathcal{M}
shows that

\mathcal{M}\cong U(\mathfrak{h})\otimes_{\mathbbm{k}}U(\mathfrak{u}^{-})

as left
U(\mathfrak{h})
-modules. In particular,
\mathcal{M}
is a free
U(\mathfrak{h})
-module and is a filtered by setting
\mathcal{M}^{\leq t}=U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq t}\otimes U(\mathfrak{u}^{-})
for
t\geq 0
. For short, given
t\geq 0
, write
\mathcal{M}^{t}
for
U(\mathfrak{h})^{t}\otimes U(\mathfrak{u}^{-})
.

10.2.
The Casimir map and filtrations

Recall that
V=V_{n}=A^{\oplus n}
denotes the natural right
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module. Recall from
Section

9.1
that for each
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module
M
there is a homomorphism

\displaystyle C=C_{M}:M\otimes V\rightarrow M\otimes V

given on homogeneous
m\in M
and
v_{t}^{\alpha}\in V
by

(10.2.1)

\displaystyle C_{M}(m\otimes v^{\alpha}_{t})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{r,t}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}mE_{r,t}^{b}\otimes v_{r}^{[{}_{1}\alpha]b^{\vee}}.

The second sum is obtained from the first by using the teleporter formula given in
Remark

9.1.2
.

Lemma 10.2.1
.

Let
\alpha\in A
and let
1\leq r,s\leq n
. Then the right action of
E_{r,s}^{\alpha}
on
\mathcal{M}
satisfies
\mathcal{M}^{t}E_{r,s}^{\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal{M}^{t}
if
r>s
, and
\mathcal{M}^{t}E_{r,s}^{\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
if
r\leq s
.

Proof.

Let
m\in\mathcal{M}^{t}
. By linearity, we may assume without loss that

m=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\otimes\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<i\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(E^{b}_{i,j}\right)^{u_{i,j,b}}

where the two products are PBW basis elements and
t=\sum_{1\leq k\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}}t_{k,b}
. If
r>s
, then since
U(\mathfrak{u}^{-})
is a subalgebra one has
mE_{r,s}^{\alpha}\in\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\otimes U(\mathfrak{u}^{-})=\mathcal{M}^{t}
, as claimed.

For
r\leq s
we argue by induction on
u:=\sum_{1\leq j<i\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}}u_{i,j,b}
.
Consider the base case of
u=0
.
If
r=s
, then

mE_{r,s}^{\alpha}=mh_{r}^{\alpha}=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\otimes 1\right)h_{r}^{\alpha}=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\right)h_{r}^{\alpha}\otimes 1

That this lies in
\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
follows from the multiplicativity of the filtration on
U(\mathfrak{h})
. If
r<s
, then

mE_{r,s}^{\alpha}=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\otimes 1\right)E_{r,s}^{\alpha}=\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}\right)E_{r,s}^{\alpha}\otimes 1=0.

Now consider the case of
u>0
. For short, let
X=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq k\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(h^{b}_{k}\right)^{t_{k,b}}
. Let
E_{p,q}^{c}
be the rightmost term in the monomial
\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<i\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(E^{b}_{i,j}\right)^{u_{i,j,b}}
. Then

\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<i\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(E^{b}_{i,j}\right)^{u_{i,j,b}}=YE_{p,q}^{c},

where
Y=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<i\leq n\\
b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}\left(E^{b}_{i,j}\right)^{u^{\prime}_{i,j,b}}
with
u^{\prime}_{p,q,c}=u_{p,q,c}-1
and
u^{\prime}_{i,j,b}=u_{i,j,b}
for all other triples
(i,j,b)
. In particular,
Y
is a PBW basis element and
u^{\prime}:=\sum_{1\leq j<i\leq n,b\in\mathtt{B}}u^{\prime}_{i,j,b}=u-1
. In this case, applying the commutator formula yields:

\displaystyle mE_{r,s}^{\alpha}

\displaystyle=X\otimes YE_{p,q}^{c}E_{r,s}^{\alpha}

\displaystyle=X\otimes Y\left((-1)^{\bar{c}\bar{\alpha}}E_{r,s}^{\alpha}E_{p,q}^{c}+\delta_{r,q}E_{p,s}^{c\alpha}-(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{c}}\delta_{s,p}E_{r,q}^{\alpha c}\right)

\displaystyle=(-1)^{\bar{c}\bar{\alpha}}X\otimes YE_{r,s}^{\alpha}E_{p,q}^{c}+\delta_{r,q}X\otimes YE_{p,s}^{c\alpha}-(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{c}}\delta_{s,p}X\otimes YE_{r,q}^{\alpha c}.

Since
u^{\prime}<u
, it follows by induction that
X\otimes YE_{r,s}^{\alpha}\in\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
and, hence,
X\otimes YE_{r,s}^{\alpha}E_{p,q}^{c}\in\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
from observing that
p>q
and applying earlier arguments. For the second term of the sum,
X\otimes YE_{p,s}^{c\alpha}\in\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
because either
p>s
and it follows from earlier arguments, or
p\leq s
and the inductive assumption applies. Identical reasoning applies to the third term. Since all three terms lie in
\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
, the claim follows.
∎

If
T
is a right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-module, then
\mathcal{M}\otimes T
is naturally a
((U(\mathfrak{h}),U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)))
-bimodule where
U(\mathfrak{h})
acts on the left on
\mathcal{M}
and
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
acts on the right via its coproduct. Furthermore,
\mathcal{M}\otimes T
is a filtered left
U(\mathfrak{h})
-module by declaring
\left(\mathcal{M}\otimes T\right)^{\leq t}=\mathcal{M}^{\leq t}\otimes T
. The next result describe how the map
C
interacts with certain filtrations of this kind.

Lemma 10.2.2
.

If
U
is a right
U(\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A))
-module, then the action of

C=C_{\mathcal{M}\otimes U}:\left(\mathcal{M}\otimes U\right)\otimes V\rightarrow\left(\mathcal{M}\otimes U\right)\otimes V

satisfies

C\left(\left(\mathcal{M}^{\leq t}\otimes U\right)\otimes V\right)\subseteq\left(\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}\otimes U\right)\otimes V

for all
t\geq 0
.

Proof.

Let
1\leq k\leq n
and
\alpha\in A
. It suffices to consider
(m\otimes u)\otimes v^{\alpha}_{k}\in\left(\mathcal{M}^{t}\otimes U\right)\otimes V
. Applying the definition of
C
along with the action of
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
on
\mathcal{M}\otimes U
yields:

\displaystyle C\left((m\otimes u)\otimes v^{\alpha}_{k}\right)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(m\otimes u)E_{r,k}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\overline{\alpha}\overline{b}+(\overline{b}+\overline{\alpha})\overline{u}}(mE_{r,k}^{b\alpha}\otimes u)\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}m\otimes\left(uE_{r,k}^{b\alpha}\right)\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}.

By
Lemma

10.2.1
the terms in the first sum lie in
\left(\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}\otimes U\right)\otimes V
and, self-evidently, the terms in the second sum lie in
\left(\mathcal{M}^{\leq t}\otimes U\right)\otimes V
. The result follows.
∎

10.3.
On the image of the Casimir operator under the defining representation

Let us establish some useful notation. Given a filtered
\mathbbm{k}
-module
T
,
t\geq 0
, and
x,y\in T
, we write

(10.3.1)

x\equiv_{t+1}y

if
x,y\in T^{\leq(t+1)}
and if
x-y\in T^{\leq t}
.

As an example of this notation that will be used later, say
c_{1},\dotsc,c_{t}\in\mathtt{B}
with
c_{1}\leq c_{2}\leq\dotsb\leq c_{t}
in our fixed ordering on
\mathtt{B}
, and set
1\leq i_{1}\leq\dotsb\leq i_{t}\leq n
. The product of
h_{i_{1}}^{c_{1}},\dotsc,h_{i_{t}}^{c_{t}}
in the given order is the unique PBW basis element of
U(\mathfrak{h})
that can be formed as a product of these elements. For any other ordering, it follows from (
10.1.4
) that

(10.3.2)

h_{i_{\tau(1)}}^{c_{\tau(1)}}\dotsb h_{i_{\tau(t)}}^{c_{\tau(t)}}\equiv_{t}\pm h_{i_{1}}^{c_{1}}\dotsb h_{i_{t}}^{c_{t}},

where
\tau\in S_{t}
and where the sign is determined by
\tau
and the parities of
c_{1},\dotsc,c_{t}
.

Lemma 10.3.1
.

Let
u\in U(\mathfrak{h})^{\leq t}
,
1\leq k\leq n
, and
\alpha\in A
. The map

C=C_{\mathcal{M}}:\mathcal{M}\otimes V\rightarrow\mathcal{M}\otimes V

satisfies

\displaystyle C\left((u\otimes 1)\otimes v_{k}^{\alpha}\right)

\displaystyle\equiv_{t+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(uh_{k}^{b\alpha}\otimes 1)\otimes v_{k}^{b^{\vee}}

\displaystyle\equiv_{t+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(uh_{k}^{b}\otimes 1)\otimes v_{k}^{({}_{1}\alpha)b^{\vee}}.

Proof.

By definition,

C((u\otimes 1)\otimes v_{k}^{\alpha})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
r\in[1,n]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(u\otimes 1)E_{r,k}^{b\alpha}\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}.

Since
(u\otimes 1)E_{r,k}^{b\alpha}=0
whenever
r<k
, we have

C((u\otimes 1)\otimes v_{t}^{\alpha})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
k=r\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(uh_{k}^{b\alpha}\otimes 1)\otimes v_{k}^{b^{\vee}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\\
1\leq k<r\leq n\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\bar{\alpha}\bar{b}}(u\otimes E_{r,k}^{b\alpha})\otimes v_{r}^{b^{\vee}}.

Since the first sum lies in
\mathcal{M}^{\leq(t+1)}
and the second sum lies in
\mathcal{M}^{\leq t}
, the first claimed
\equiv_{t+1}
follows. The second formula is argued in the same fashion using the other formula for
C
given in
Eq.

10.2.1
.
∎

1\leq k\leq d
, let

By local finiteness,
C_{k}
and
\sigma_{p,q}
give well-defined endomorphisms
C_{k,M}
and
\sigma_{p,q,M}
, respectively, of
M\otimes V^{\otimes d}
for any
\mathfrak{gl}_{n}(A)
-module
M
. Moreover, on
\mathcal{M}\otimes V^{\otimes d}
, the map given by
\sigma_{p,q}
only acts on the vectors of
V^{\otimes d}
and, hence, preserves filtration degrees.

Lemma 10.3.2
.

Let
u\in U(\mathfrak{h})^{t}
,
1\leq k\leq d
, and
\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{d}\in A
. Then the map

C_{k}=C_{k,\mathcal{M}}:\mathcal{M}\otimes V^{\otimes d}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}\otimes V^{\otimes d}

satisfies

\displaystyle C_{k}\left((u\otimes 1)\otimes v_{t_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{t_{d}}^{\alpha_{d}}\right)

\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt\equiv_{t+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in\mathtt{B}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\overline{\alpha}_{k}\overline{b}+\overline{b}(\overline{\alpha}_{1}+\dotsb+\overline{\alpha}_{k-1})}(uh_{t_{k}}^{b}\otimes 1)\otimes v_{t_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{t_{k}}^{({}_{1}\alpha_{k})b^{\vee}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes v_{t_{d}}^{\alpha_{d}}

Proof.

Consider
C_{k}-\sigma_{1,k}C_{1}\sigma_{1,k}
. It follows from repeated applications of
Lemma

5.3.1
that this can be written as a linear combination of webs that have no affine dots. These webs act only on the vectors in
V^{\otimes d}
and, hence, preserve filtration degree when they act on
\mathcal{M}\otimes V^{\otimes d}
. Therefore, to prove the asserted formulas it suffices to prove them when
C_{k}
is replaced by
\sigma_{1,k}C_{1}\sigma_{1,k}
. But this case follows from the fact that
C_{1}=C_{\mathcal{M}}\otimes{\rm Id}_{V}^{\otimes(d-1)}
, the previous lemma, and that
\sigma_{1,k}
acts on
V^{\otimes d}
by signed place permutation.
∎
